ijCSCL_4_1_2.title: Productive failure in CSCL groups
ijCSCL_4_1_2.summary_ollama: This study investigated the productive failure hypothesis, which suggests that students who experience failure while working on ill-structured problems in a collaborative learning environment may outperform their peers who worked on well-structured problems. The researchers randomly assigned 177 11th-grade science students to either an ill-structured problem-solving condition or a well-structured problem-solving condition and found that the students in the ill-structured condition performed significantly better on both the well-structured and ill-structured posttests, demonstrating confirmatory evidence for the productive failure hypothesis.
ijCSCL_4_1_2.summary_haiku: Groups solving unstructured physics problems without support struggled initially but subsequently outperformed peers who solved well-structured problems on individual transfer tasks. This confirmatory study with 177 eleventh-grade students demonstrates productive failure: complex, divergent collaborative processes seemingly leading to failure paradoxically enhanced later problem-solving performance, suggesting that the nature of collaborative interaction rather than prior knowledge or solution quality drives learning gains.

ijCSCL_5_3_5.title: Revealing preconditions for trustful collaboration in CSCL
ijCSCL_5_3_5.summary_haiku: This philosophical analysis examines preconditions for trust in virtual learning environments. Through phenomenological inquiry and case analysis, the author argues that self-surrender—fundamental to human communication—is undermined by surveillance and impression management in online learning systems. Drawing on open-source community models, the study concludes that volunteerism, self-articulation of goals, and inquiry-based teaching methods can foster mastery-oriented learning and authentic collaborative engagement.

ijCSCL_10_3_4.title: Group-level formative feedback and metadiscourse
ijCSCL_10_3_4.authors: Monica Resendes1 & Marlene Scardamalia1 & Carl Bereiter1 & Bodong Chen2 & Cindy Halewood3
ijCSCL_10_3_4.summary_haiku: Grade 2 students engaged in knowledge building with visualization-based formative feedback tools showed significant improvements in domain vocabulary use, scientific accuracy, explanation complexity, and discourse connectivity compared to a comparison class. Using comparative word clouds and epistemic discourse move graphs, students demonstrated productive metadiscourse—reflection on their collective knowledge-building process—though primarily with teacher facilitation, suggesting young children possess greater metacognitive capacity than typically assumed.

ijCSCL_6_2_5.title: A multimodal approach to coding discourse: Collaboration, distributed cognition, and geometric reasoning
ijCSCL_6_2_5.authors: Michael A. Evans & Eliot Feenstra & Emily Ryon & David McNeill
ijCSCL_6_2_5.summary_haiku: Researchers developed a multimodal coding framework to analyze distributed cognition in young children's collaborative problem-solving. Using speech, gesture, and gaze analysis, they tracked "coreferences"—shared references to objects, participants, and concepts—across three discourse levels. Applied to 7-8-year-olds solving tangrams physically and virtually, findings revealed increased meta-level communication and coalition formation in computer-supported settings, with dominant participants showing greater influence in virtual versus physical environments.

ijCSCL_4_3_0.title: Classical dialogs in CSCL
ijCSCL_4_3_0.summary_haiku: This editorial reviews the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning's progress and synthesizes key research themes from the 2009 CSCL conference. It examines diverse analytical methodologies for studying collaborative learning processes, including event-centered approaches, knowledge creation discourse analysis, and interaction analysis in dual-interaction environments. The authors highlight fundamental tensions between individual and community-level learning, emphasizing how CSCL research must integrate multiple theoretical perspectives and analytical approaches to understand complex collaborative learning phenomena.

ijCSCL_7_2_0.title: Cognizing mediating: Unpacking the entanglement of artifacts with collective minds
ijCSCL_7_2_0.summary_haiku: Human cognition and technological artifacts mutually shape each other through dialectical processes. This editorial examines instrumental genesis theory—how artifacts evolve through use—comparing it with affordances and structuration theories. The analysis emphasizes that CSCL research should focus on small-group collective cognition, design complex collaborative tasks beyond individual capability, and employ multiple methodologies to understand how groups enact technological mediation during knowledge building.

ijCSCL_6_4_3.title: Interfering and resolving: How tabletop interaction facilitates co-construction of argumentative knowledge
ijCSCL_6_4_3.summary_haiku: Peer interference in shared tabletop interfaces can productively support argumentative knowledge co-construction during exploratory science learning. Analyzing 43 students aged 11-14 interacting with a tangible light-behavior simulation, researchers applied Weinberger and Fischer's consensus-building framework to interference episodes. Integration-oriented consensus building—where students reflected on and incorporated peers' contributions—consistently produced productive learning, while conflict-oriented approaches typically yielded counter-productive outcomes.

ijCSCL_6_4_2.title: Multi-touch tables and the relationship with collaborative classroom pedagogies: A synthetic review
ijCSCL_6_4_2.authors: Steven E. Higgins & Emma Mercier & Elizabeth Burd & Andrew Hatch
ijCSCL_6_4_2.summary_haiku: Multi-touch tables offer significant potential for supporting collaborative classroom learning through their design features. This synthetic review proposes a typology categorizing hardware characteristics—surface geometry and display type, touch sensing capabilities, and connectivity—to analyze how technical affordances align with pedagogical goals. Evidence suggests horizontal multi-touch surfaces enable more equitable participation and task-focused interaction than traditional single-touch technologies, though text entry limitations and teacher orchestration challenges require further investigation.

ijCSCL_7_2_1.title: Connecting agents and artifacts in CSCL: Towards a rationale of mutual shaping
ijCSCL_7_2_1.authors: Maarten Overdijk & Wouter van Diggelen & Paul A. Kirschner & Michael Baker
ijCSCL_7_2_1.summary_haiku: This article examines how human agents and technical artifacts connect in computer-supported collaborative learning. Through theoretical review of affordance, structuration, and instrumental genesis frameworks, the authors argue that existing CSCL research emphasizing artifact-driven "shaping" of collaboration should shift toward "mutual shaping," where both learners and technologies reciprocally influence each other. Instrumental genesis emerges as the most viable theoretical approach for understanding this bidirectional relationship.

ijCSCL_4_3_1.title: Time is precious: Variable- and event-centred approaches to process analysis in CSCL research
ijCSCL_4_3_1.summary_haiku: CSCL research often neglects temporal dimensions despite studying processes unfolding over weeks or months. Reimann argues that variable-centered variance theory inadequately captures long-term change, proposing event-centered analysis as a complementary approach. Event-based methods enable narrative explanation, accommodate multiple causality types, and facilitate integration of qualitative and quantitative analyses, offering CSCL researchers more appropriate tools for analyzing extended collaborative learning processes.

ijCSCL_6_2_4.title: Comparing the effects of representational tools in collaborative and individual inquiry learning
ijCSCL_6_2_4.authors: Bas Kolloffel & Tessa H. S. Eysink & Ton de Jong
ijCSCL_6_2_4.summary_haiku: Collaborative learners significantly outperformed individual learners in combinatorics and probability inquiry learning, particularly on intuitive and situational knowledge. Using a pre-test/post-test design with 61 collaborative dyads and 95 individual students, three representational tool formats (conceptual, arithmetical, textual) were compared. Results showed collaboration's benefits persisted regardless of tool use, while individual learners benefited from externalization. Representational format did not directly enhance specific knowledge types as hypothesized, though approximately 50% adopted conceptual or textual tools versus only 20% using arithmetical formats.

ijCSCL_5_3_4.title: S-COL: A Copernican turn for the development of flexibly reusable collaboration scripts
ijCSCL_5_3_4.authors: Christof Wecker & Karsten Stegmann & Florian Bernstein & Michael J. Huber & Georg Kalus & Ingo Kollar & Sabine Rathmayer & Frank Fischer
ijCSCL_5_3_4.summary_haiku: S-COL is a browser-based tool enabling flexible reuse of collaboration scripts across diverse web-based learning platforms. Rather than embedding scripts within specific platforms, S-COL implements scripts in the browser and triggers them by recognizing functionally equivalent page types. An empirical study demonstrated that a collaboration script for online search implemented in S-COL effectively increased students' engagement in early-stage search activities, supporting the tool's feasibility for sustainable script development and reuse.

ijCSCL_4_1_3.title: A connective ethnography of peer knowledge sharing and diffusion in a tween virtual world
ijCSCL_4_1_3.authors: Deborah A. Fields & Yasmin B. Kafai
ijCSCL_4_1_3.summary_haiku: Researchers used connective ethnography to trace how tweens ages 9-12 learned and shared an insider gaming practice—teleporting—across an after-school club, classrooms, and the virtual world Whyville.net. Integrating video, field notes, logfiles, and interviews, they found that most participants traversed multiple physical and virtual spaces to learn this practice, employing observation, questioning, and peer coaching. Knowledge diffusion occurred through informal, unstructured interactions rather than explicit instruction, demonstrating how virtual spaces expand peer-to-peer learning opportunities beyond traditional classroom boundaries.

ijCSCL_4_1_1.title: The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies
ijCSCL_4_1_1.summary_haiku: # Summary Collaborative technologies rarely address formal learning needs despite their educational potential. This paper proposes the Conversational Framework—a pedagogical model integrating instructionism, constructionism, socio-cultural, and collaborative learning theories—to establish user requirements for technology design. The framework emphasizes iterative interactions between teachers, learners, and peers across discursive and experiential levels, enabling educators to challenge technologies to deliver genuinely enhanced learning rather than merely digitizing conventional methods.

ijCSCL_6_2_6.title: Designing automated adaptive support to improve student helping behaviors in a peer tutoring activity
ijCSCL_6_2_6.authors: Erin Walker & Nikol Rummel & Kenneth R. Koedinger
ijCSCL_6_2_6.summary_haiku: Researchers used a four-phase iterative design process to develop adaptive support for peer tutoring in algebra. Through user needs analysis, system design, classroom experimentation, and qualitative case analysis, they found that adaptive assistance improved conceptual help quality and sentence classifier usage compared to fixed support, though learning gains were not significantly different. The study demonstrates how accountability-focused design principles can enhance collaborative help-giving behaviors.

ijCSCL_5_1_4.title: Toward a dialectic relation between the results in CSCL: Three critical methodological aspects of content analysis schemes
ijCSCL_5_1_4.summary_haiku: This paper proposes a framework of indicators based on three critical methodological aspects—units of analysis, relations between theoretical levels, and dimensions of analysis—to facilitate reciprocal positioning of content analysis results in CSCL research. Rather than seeking theoretical integration across diverse approaches, the authors argue for dialectical relations that reveal tensions and enable mutual theoretical development within the field's inherent methodological diversity.

ijCSCL_4_3_3.title: A three-level analysis of collaborative learning in dual-interaction spaces
ijCSCL_4_3_3.summary_haiku: This article presents a three-level qualitative interaction analysis methodology for dual-interaction spaces—CSCL systems combining shared artifact editing with synchronous communication. The approach analyzes collaborative learning traces at dialog, knowledge, and action levels to identify patterns and inform system customization. Applied to software engineering diagram construction, the method reveals how learners negotiate categorization rules through prototypical examples, enabling evidence-based improvements to learning environment design.

ijCSCL_7_2_3.title: Instrumental genesis in technology-mediated learning: From double stimulation to expansive knowledge practices
ijCSCL_7_2_3.summary_haiku: Technology-mediated collaborative learning requires transforming social practices through instrumental genesis—the developmental process of appropriating technological tools as learning instruments. Drawing on sociocultural theory, the authors argue that epistemic mediation through external artifacts enables knowledge creation, but productive integration demands extended iterative efforts reformatting cognitive-cultural operating systems at personal and collective levels, explaining why innovative CSCL practices remain difficult to implement in educational systems.

ijCSCL_7_4_5.title: A model for flexibly editing CSCL scripts
ijCSCL_7_4_5.summary_haiku: Researchers developed the T2 model, a table-tree representation system enabling teachers to flexibly edit CSCL scripts. Using intuitive table structures mapped to machine-readable trees, the approach prioritizes simplicity and adaptability over complex meta-models. Usability testing with five teachers confirmed the model's ease of use and demonstrated that teachers effectively leveraged representation flexibility to customize scripts according to their perspectives and contexts.

ijCSCL_6_4_0.title: Collaborating around the tabletop
ijCSCL_6_4_0.summary_haiku: Tabletop computing environments can serve as focal points for collaborative learning by integrating physical and digital artifacts, spoken and written texts, and computational support. This editorial introduces a flash theme examining how tabletop interfaces support small-group interaction, exploring design considerations, interaction patterns, scripted collaboration, and community building across diverse educational contexts.

ijCSCL_6_4_1.title: Interactive tabletops in education
ijCSCL_6_4_1.summary_haiku: Interactive tabletops support co-located collaborative learning through hands-on manipulation of objects, conveying socio-constructivist pedagogical approaches. This analytical framework examines 33 design considerations across four levels: user-system interaction, teamwork dynamics, classroom orchestration, and socio-cultural contexts. The authors argue that tabletops' educational effectiveness depends on thoughtful design addressing these specific affordances rather than inherent technological properties.

ijCSCL_7_4_4.title: Participatory learning through behavioral and cognitive engagements in an online collective information searching activity
ijCSCL_7_4_4.summary_haiku: This study investigated how college students' behavioral and cognitive engagements relate during online collective information searching using social bookmarking. Through cluster analysis of 101 engineering students' activity logs and annotations, researchers identified four behavioral patterns (Hitchhiker, Individualist, Active, Commentator) and two cognitive levels (Deep, Surface). Results revealed that students exhibiting "Active" behavioral engagement demonstrated "Deep" cognitive engagement, while those with "Hitchhiker" or "Individualist" patterns showed "Surface" engagement, with deeper engagement correlating to better assignment performance.

ijCSCL_7_2_2.title: An instrumental perspective on CSCL systems
ijCSCL_7_2_2.summary_haiku: Rabardel's instrumental genesis theory reveals that CSCL systems involve complex two-phase development: teachers customize artifacts during preparation, while learners and tutors collaboratively develop utilization schemes during use. The research distinguishes two system categories based on who drives instrumentalization—learner-instrumentalizable systems supporting emergent collaborative practices, and teacher-instrumentalizable systems enforcing predefined learning structures—each mediating different forms of knowledge construction through epistemic, pragmatic, interpersonal, and reflexive mediation.

ijCSCL_10_1_4.title: Appropriation of a representational tool in a second-language classroom
ijCSCL_10_1_4.authors: Yun Wen & Chee-Kit Looi & Wenli Chen
ijCSCL_10_1_4.summary_ollama: This study investigates how small groups of students appropriate a representational tool for facilitating collaborative L2 learning in authentic classrooms. The results indicate that group language proficiency and task design influence the way the representational tool is appropriated, with inscriptional devices playing significant roles in group-understanding development. The findings suggest that the representational tool can facilitate equal participation, empower learners to be aware of their language problems, and serve as resources for the emergence of new ideas/perspectives.
ijCSCL_10_1_4.summary_haiku: This case study examined how secondary school students appropriated Group Scribbles, a representational tool, during collaborative Chinese-language writing in a networked classroom. Through microanalysis of cross-media interactions between face-to-face and online spaces, researchers identified five functions inscriptional devices served in group-understanding development: referencing, pinpointing, prompting notice, realizing parallels, and promoting synergy. Findings revealed that representational tools supplement face-to-face communication by enabling balanced participation, helping learners notice linguistic problems, and serving as resources for elaborating ideas.

ijCSCL_4_3_2.title: Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge- construction, and knowledge-creation discourses Jan van Aalst
ijCSCL_4_3_2.summary_haiku: This study distinguishes three discourse modes—knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge creation—using a coding scheme applied to secondary students' asynchronous online discussions in Knowledge Forum about SARS and Avian Flu. Analysis of four student groups' discourses revealed one group engaged in knowledge-creation discourse with superior knowledge advancement, one in knowledge-sharing discourse, and two in hybrid modes. Community sense emerged as the primary differentiating factor.

ijCSCL_6_2_7.title: CSCL for intellectually disabled pupils: Stimulating interaction by using a floor control mechanism
ijCSCL_6_2_7.authors: Ulrike Cress & Katrin Wodzicki & Martina Bientzle & Andreas Lingnau
ijCSCL_6_2_7.summary_haiku: This study examined whether floor control mechanisms—restricting simultaneous actions in collaborative learning environments—improve interaction quality for intellectually disabled pupils. Twenty pupils completed a furniture-sorting task in pairs using tablet PCs, comparing floor control versus unrestricted conditions. Results showed floor control reduced relocations, decreased coordinative communication, and increased content-related discussion, particularly when pupils disagreed or faced difficult symbols, while producing slightly higher-quality collaborative outcomes.

ijCSCL_4_1_0.title: Yes we can!
ijCSCL_4_1_0.summary_haiku: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) offers transformative potential for education by moving beyond traditional knowledge transfer to engage students in collaborative knowledge construction with peers. This editorial argues that CSCL systems, when fully developed, can provide effective learning environments supporting cross-border collaboration while preparing students for an increasingly global, interdependent world.

ijCSCL_5_3_3.title: How digital concept maps about the collaborators’ knowledge and information influence computer-supported collaborative problem solving
ijCSCL_5_3_3.summary_haiku: Digital concept maps displaying collaborators' knowledge structures and information resources enhance computer-supported collaborative problem-solving. This experimental study compared 40 triads—20 with access to partners' concept maps and 20 without—on problem-solving tasks. Results demonstrated that groups with map access acquired greater knowledge-and-information awareness, focused on problem-relevant information, and solved problems faster and more accurately than control groups.

ijCSCL_4_1_4.title: Learning to collaborate while being scripted or by observing a model
ijCSCL_4_1_4.authors: Nikol Rummel & Hans Spada & Sabine Hauser
ijCSCL_4_1_4.summary_haiku: Observing a worked-out collaboration model with elaboration support proved most effective for improving computer-mediated collaborative problem-solving among medical and psychology students. Using an experimental design with five conditions, researchers found that model-based learning outperformed scripted collaboration on process quality and knowledge measures. Results challenge the prevailing positive view of collaboration scripts in CSCL research, suggesting adaptive scripting approaches instead.

ijCSCL_6_2_3.title: An information processing perspective on divergence and convergence in collaborative learning Robert L. Jorczak
ijCSCL_6_2_3.summary_haiku: Jorczak proposes a Collaborative Information Processing (CIP) model explaining how peer discussion facilitates learning through information divergence and convergence. Using information processing theory, the model demonstrates that groups benefit from diverse member perspectives triggering conceptual conflict, followed by convergent processes achieving shared understanding. The CIP framework unifies cognitive and social interaction theories, predicting that heterogeneous groups and divergent information exchange enhance collaborative learning outcomes.

ijCSCL_10_3_2.title: Learning to learn together with CSCL tools
ijCSCL_10_3_2.authors: Baruch B. Schwarz1 & Reuma de Groot1 & Manolis Mavrikis2 & Toby Dragon3
ijCSCL_10_3_2.summary_haiku: This design-based research study introduces Learning to Learn Together (L2L2)—learning to collaborate while engaging in inquiry and argumentation on challenging tasks. Using the Metafora CSCL platform integrating planning tools, microworlds, and discussion features, researchers observed three classroom cases where students developed collaborative practices including collective reflection, mutual engagement, and peer assessment. Results demonstrate L2L2 is an attainable educational goal, partially achieved through technology-mediated affordances supporting integrated inquiry-argumentation-collaboration practices.

ijCSCL_5_1_1.title: A framework for conceptualizing, representing, and analyzing distributed interaction
ijCSCL_5_1_1.authors: Daniel D. Suthers & Nathan Dwyer & Richard Medina & Ravi Vatrapu
ijCSCL_5_1_1.summary_haiku: # Summary Suthers and colleagues present an uptake analysis framework for analyzing distributed technology-mediated interaction. The framework uses contingency graphs—abstract transcripts representing events as vertices and relationships between events as edges—to unify interaction data across multiple media and temporal scales. Uptake, defined as participants taking prior events as relevant for ongoing activity, serves as the conceptual foundation. The authors demonstrate the framework's utility through qualitative and quantitative analyses of synchronous and asynchronous collaborative learning data, arguing it enables both microanalysis and scaled statistical analysis while supporting dialogue across diverse CSCL methodologies.

ijCSCL_7_2_6.title: Scripted collaborative learning with the cognitive tutor algebra
ijCSCL_7_2_6.authors: Nikol Rummel & Dejana Mullins & Hans Spada
ijCSCL_7_2_6.summary_haiku: Researchers extended the Cognitive Tutor Algebra system to support collaborative learning by implementing a jigsaw-based collaboration script with adaptive elements. In a classroom experiment comparing scripted collaboration, unscripted collaboration, and individual learning, process analyses revealed the script improved interaction quality and problem-solving during learning. However, quantitative between-condition comparisons showed no significant learning advantage for collaboration, though collaborative performance matched individual performance despite fewer practice problems, suggesting interaction compensated for reduced practice opportunities.

ijCSCL_10_1_0.title: From the editors: Collaboration and the formation of new knowledge artifacts
ijCSCL_10_1_0.authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Ulrike Cress
ijCSCL_10_1_0.summary_ollama: This article explores the formation and alignment of new knowledge artifacts in collaborative learning contexts, highlighting the interplay between conceptual and material structures. The authors introduce a framework for understanding how artifacts are formed and refined through collaboration, emphasizing the importance of intersubjective meaning-making and the role of artifacts as mediators between individual understanding and community institutions.
ijCSCL_10_1_0.summary_haiku: Computer-supported collaborative learning fundamentally involves creating and refining knowledge artifacts—physical or virtual objects embodying shared meanings. This editorial examines how collaborative technologies enable students to construct intersubjective understanding through artifacts like augmented-reality environments, texts, visualizations, and networked tools, emphasizing that productive learning emerges from alignment between conceptual resources and material structures during collaborative interaction.

ijCSCL_7_4_0.title: Traversing planes of learning
ijCSCL_7_4_0.summary_haiku: CSCL research typically analyzes learning at three interconnected but separately studied levels: individual, small-group, and community. This article argues that understanding how these planes interpenetrate requires examining artifacts and resources that mediate across levels. Using bridge metaphors and phenomenological theory, Stahl proposes that collaborative knowledge-building involves sequential interaction drawing resources from all planes, with designed artifacts and language serving as key connectors enabling traversal between learning levels.

ijCSCL_6_4_5.title: Guided reciprocal questioning to support children’s collaborative storytelling
ijCSCL_6_4_5.authors: Giulia Gelmini-Hornsby & Shaaron Ainsworth & Claire O’Malley
ijCSCL_6_4_5.summary_haiku: Guided Reciprocal Peer Questioning (GRPQ) scripts significantly enhance children's collaborative storytelling through increased interactive discussion. Using a within-subjects design with 36 six-to-seven-year-olds creating stories with KidPad, the study found that question prompts promoted longer, more evaluatively rich, and more coherent stories. Benefits largely persisted after scaffold withdrawal, suggesting children internalized the questioning approach and can apply it independently.

ijCSCL_6_4_4.title: Collaboration within large groups in the classroom
ijCSCL_6_4_4.authors: Eyal Szewkis & Miguel Nussbaum & Tal Rosen & Jose Abalos & Fernanda Denardin & Daniela Caballero & Arturo Tagle & Cristian Alcoholado
ijCSCL_6_4_4.summary_haiku: This study investigates large-group classroom collaboration using Single Display Groupware with multiple mice and minimal hardware. Through an experimental design comparing 42 students using the system for 40% of class time against 32 control students, researchers found that "silent collaboration"—a negotiation mechanism enabling object exchanges—effectively facilitated synchronous learning in Spanish language tasks. Results demonstrated significant learning gains and successful achievement of collaborative conditions, suggesting this low-cost approach enables effective large-group computer-supported collaborative learning.

ijCSCL_7_4_1.title: Computational analysis and mapping of ijCSCL content
ijCSCL_7_4_1.summary_haiku: This empirical study employs co-word analysis to map content in the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2006-2011). Using hierarchical clustering and multidimensional scaling on full-text corpora, the research identifies three major thematic categories: interaction analysis, technical/organizational issues, and applications. Key findings include dominant themes like scripting, monitoring, community-based learning, and argumentation, revealing the intellectual structure of CSCL research.

ijCSCL_10_1_1.title: Constructing liminal blends in a collaborative augmented-reality learning environment
ijCSCL_10_1_1.authors: Noel Enyedy & Joshua A. Danish & David DeLiema
ijCSCL_10_1_1.summary_ollama: This study examines how augmented reality (AR) environments support learning through the concept of liminal blends, which are publicly co-constructed conceptual integrations that combine multiple resources from different spaces to produce new inferences. The authors analyze a case study of second-grade students using an AR system to learn about friction and motion, and identify three stages of blending: composition, completion, and elaboration. They argue that the liminal blend framework provides a theory and methodology for understanding how students co-construct meaning from within AR environments, and can inform the design of future AR learning environments.
ijCSCL_10_1_1.summary_haiku: This study examines how augmented-reality environments support physics learning through "liminal blends"—conceptual integrations of students' embodied experiences, physical materials, peer contributions, and symbolic representations. Using interaction analysis of second-graders learning about friction, the researchers demonstrate how students blend their bodies, game narratives, material surfaces, and AR symbols to reason about force and motion, revealing cognition as distributed across individuals, materials, and social interaction.

ijCSCL_5_1_0.title: The CSCL field matures
ijCSCL_5_1_0.summary_haiku: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) has matured as a field, evidenced by the International Journal of CSCL's acceptance into Thomson Reuters' Web of Science indexing. This editorial reflects on the field's institutional growth since 1989, highlighting how current research demonstrates increased theoretical sophistication, methodological rigor, and productive engagement across diverse disciplinary perspectives within CSCL scholarship.

ijCSCL_10_3_3.title: Collaborative group engagement in a computer-supported inquiry learning environment
ijCSCL_10_3_3.authors: Suparna Sinha1 & Toni Kempler Rogat2 & Karlyn R. Adams-Wiggins1 & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver3
ijCSCL_10_3_3.summary_haiku: This study develops an observational protocol to measure collaborative group engagement in computer-supported inquiry learning as multifaceted—encompassing behavioral, social, cognitive, and conceptual-to-consequential dimensions. Using qualitative analysis of ten middle school groups solving an ecosystem problem, researchers found that behavioral and social engagement differentiated low-quality groups, while cognitive and conceptual-to-consequential engagement characterized high-quality engagement. Results demonstrate these engagement facets are highly interrelated and mutually influential, with implications for designing technologies that scaffold deeper learning in collaborative environments.

ijCSCL_6_2_2.title: Wiki-supported collaborative learning in primary education: How a dialogic space is created for thinking together
ijCSCL_6_2_2.summary_haiku: This study examined how wikis support primary students' collaborative knowledge construction through a dialogic lens. Twenty-five students engaged in a science project using MediaWiki, combining asynchronous wiki interaction with synchronous face-to-face collaboration. Analysis revealed students developed exploratory, cumulative, and disputational talk patterns, establishing intersubjective understanding. The collaborative wiki text demonstrated greater complexity, length, and reasoning than initial individual proposals, supporting the claim that dialogic approaches enhance wiki-based collaborative learning.

ijCSCL_4_1_5.title: The power of natural frameworks: Technology and the question of agency in CSCL settings
ijCSCL_4_1_5.summary_haiku: # Summary This study analyzes how secondary school students frame computer-supported collaborative learning situations using video analysis of mathematics problem-solving with educational software. Results reveal students shift between social frameworks where they assume responsibility for understanding tasks and natural frameworks where they attribute difficulties to technology design. When receiving incorrect feedback without explanation, students often cease engaging with mathematical reasoning and instead attempt procedural workarounds, potentially avoiding accountability for learning while preserving self-esteem.

ijCSCL_5_3_2.title: Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools
ijCSCL_5_3_2.authors: Jingyan Lu & Susanne P. Lajoie & Jeffrey Wiseman
ijCSCL_5_3_2.summary_haiku: Interactive whiteboards fundamentally altered teacher scaffolding in medical problem-based learning. This case study compared traditional whiteboard versus interactive whiteboard conditions during deteriorating patient simulations with medical students. Results revealed that interactive whiteboards enabled teachers to visualize all student groups' work simultaneously, allowing them to increase problem complexity and reduce task-structuring guidance. Technology expanded scaffolding choices by externalizing collaborative problem-solving processes.

ijCSCL_5_3_0.title: Guiding group cognition in CSCL
ijCSCL_5_3_0.summary_haiku: # Summary CSCL research aims to understand how multiple individuals coalesce into coherent group cognition through collaborative learning. This article examines theoretical frameworks and empirical studies investigating influences on group interaction, including scaffolding strategies, technology support, knowledge sharing mechanisms, and interpersonal trust. The research demonstrates that effective collaboration requires careful attention to sequential interaction, contextual factors, and internal preconditions for productive teamwork.

ijCSCL_6_2_0.title: Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend
ijCSCL_6_2_0.summary_haiku: This editorial argues that the CSCL field benefits from diverse theoretical, methodological, and pedagogical approaches rather than convergence on single paradigms. The authors advocate for pluralism in research perspectives, illustrating how multiple schools of thought—from dialogical to information-processing frameworks—advance understanding of collaborative learning. They present diverse studies examining practice, theory, analysis methods, and technology design, demonstrating that CSCL's complexity requires multifaceted inquiry.

ijCSCL_10_3_1.title: A Habermasian perspective on joint meaning making online: What does it offer and what are the difficulties?
ijCSCL_10_3_1.summary_haiku: Habermas's theory of communicative action—emphasizing genuine consensus through unconstrained dialogue where only "the better argument" prevails—offers a critical framework for understanding online meaning-making. This theoretical perspective values truth-seeking over technological affordances, distinguishes emancipatory from strategic communication, and interrogates techno-romantic assumptions. However, challenges include abstractness, limited practical guidance, and questions about consensus feasibility.

ijCSCL_4_3_5.title: Web 2.0: Inherent tensions and evident challenges for education
ijCSCL_4_3_5.summary_haiku: Web 2.0 practices and educational systems embody fundamentally incompatible learning metaphors. While Web 2.0 emphasizes participatory, distributed knowledge construction with internal goals, education prioritizes individual knowledge acquisition for external purposes. This conceptual tension manifests practically in challenges regarding collaboration, evaluation criteria, and material authenticity when Web 2.0 tools are integrated into educational settings.

ijCSCL_5_1_2.title: Computer-supported argumentation: A review of the state of the art
ijCSCL_5_1_2.authors: Oliver Scheuer & Frank Loll & Niels Pinkwart & Bruce M. McLaren
ijCSCL_5_1_2.summary_haiku: Computer-supported argumentation systems have evolved over 15-20 years to support and teach argumentation skills across domains. This literature review examines 50 systems, analyzing argument representations, interaction designs, ontologies, automated analysis techniques, and empirical findings. Key results show that visual representations and structured interaction designs improve argumentative discourse, while macro-level pedagogical scripts enhance learning outcomes. However, conflicting empirical results reveal the need for comprehensive theoretical frameworks and systematic comparative studies.

ijCSCL_7_2_5.title: The ACODEA framework: Developing segmentation and classification schemes for fully automatic analysis of online discussions
ijCSCL_7_2_5.authors: Jin Mu & Karsten Stegmann & Elijah Mayfield & Carolyn Rosé & Frank Fischer
ijCSCL_7_2_5.summary_haiku: The ACODEA framework enables fully automatic analysis of online discussions by extracting syntactic and semantic features through part-of-speech tagging and named-entity recognition before segmentation and classification. Applied to 84 students' collaborative discussions about attribution theory, the three-layer approach achieved high reliability (Cohen's Kappa ≥0.81) for micro-argumentation coding across different contexts, demonstrating that context-independent automated analysis is feasible for collaborative learning environments.

ijCSCL_10_1_3.title: BWhoa! We’re going deep in the trees!^: Patterns of collaboration around an interactive information visualization exhibit
ijCSCL_10_1_3.authors: Pryce Davis & Michael Horn & Florian Block & Brenda Phillips & E. Margaret Evans & Judy Diamond & Chia Shen
ijCSCL_10_1_3.summary_ollama: This study examines how dyads interact with an interactive tabletop exhibit called DeepTree, which visualizes a phylogenetic tree of life containing over 70,000 species. The researchers identified four distinct patterns of interaction: reactive, autonomous, planning, and contemplative, organized along two dimensions: coordination and target of action. They found that the most common pattern was reactive, characterized by low coordination and mechanical goals, while the least common was contemplative, marked by high coordination and conceptual goals. The study suggests that designers can support learning through each pattern by incorporating features such as gentle guidance, personal objects for independent action, and what-if explorations.
ijCSCL_10_1_3.summary_haiku: This study analyzed how child dyads collaboratively explored DeepTree, an interactive multi-touch tabletop exhibit visualizing 70,000+ species in a phylogenetic tree. Using qualitative interaction analysis of museum visitors, researchers identified four distinct collaboration patterns organized by coordination level and action target: reactive, autonomous, planning, and contemplative. Results showed that DeepTree supported learning of macroevolutionary concepts like common descent, with design features like the "fly-through" mechanic facilitating meaning-making across different interaction patterns.

ijCSCL_7_4_3.title: Using augmented reality and knowledge-building scaffolds to improve learning in a science museum
ijCSCL_7_4_3.authors: Susan A. Yoon & Karen Elinich & Joyce Wang & Christopher Steinmeier & Sean Tucker
ijCSCL_7_4_3.summary_haiku: A quasi-experimental study examined how augmented reality and knowledge-building scaffolds enhance science learning in a museum setting. Using four conditions with varying levels of digital augmentation and pedagogical support, researchers tested 119 middle-grade students on electrical conductivity concepts. Results showed digital augmentation alone improved conceptual knowledge, while knowledge-building scaffolds combined with augmented reality significantly enhanced students' ability to theorize about scientific phenomena, suggesting collaborative supports amplify technology-based informal learning.

ijCSCL_2_2_8.title: Argumentation in a changing world
ijCSCL_2_2_8.authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Reuma De Groot
ijCSCL_2_2_8.summary_haiku: # Summary This design-based research study examined a seven-month history course using the Kishurim program, which promotes critical reasoning through dialogic argumentation supported by the Digalo graphic tool. While traditional measures of argumentative components showed no significant improvement, students demonstrated significant gains in openness, coherence, and decisiveness. Analysis of e-discussions revealed that these criteria better reflect the program's dialogic pedagogical principles than conventional skill-based metrics, suggesting new evaluation standards for collaborative learning environments.

ijCSCL_6_4_6.title: Scaffolding of small groups’ metacognitive activities with an avatar
ijCSCL_6_4_6.authors: Inge Molenaar & Ming Ming Chiu & Peter Sleegers & Carla van Boxtel
ijCSCL_6_4_6.summary_haiku: Avatar-based metacognitive scaffolding in small group learning environments influences student knowledge acquisition through mediation by metacognitive activities. Multivariate multilevel analysis of 51,339 conversation turns from 54 elementary students revealed that problematizing scaffolds (eliciting student explanations) produced greater domain knowledge than structuring scaffolds (providing examples), with metacognitive activities mediating these effects. Both scaffold types enhanced metacognitive knowledge primarily through increased metacognitive engagement.

ijCSCL_6_4_7.title: Building a community among teachers, researchers and university students. A blended approach to training
ijCSCL_6_4_7.authors: Donatella Cesareni & Francesca Martini & Ilaria Mancini
ijCSCL_6_4_7.summary_haiku: # Summary This case study examined a blended learning community of 45 Italian teachers, researchers, and university students participating in the ITCOLE project. Using qualitative analysis of face-to-face and online interactions, researchers found that expert teachers assumed central roles while novice teachers engaged in legitimate peripheral participation, gradually becoming more competent community members. Teachers recognized CSCL's innovative potential for student motivation and collaborative knowledge building, though they identified challenges including technical infrastructure limitations and heavy workload demands.

ijCSCL_2_2_9.title: Rainbow: A framework for analysing computer-mediated pedagogical debates
ijCSCL_2_2_9.authors: Michael Baker & Jerry Andriessen & Kristine Lund & Marie van Amelsvoort & Matthieu Quignard
ijCSCL_2_2_9.summary_haiku: Rainbow is a seven-category analytical framework for analyzing computer-mediated pedagogical debates in CSCL environments. Developed through pragma-dialectical theory and dialogue analysis, it identifies when students broaden and deepen understanding of debate spaces through argumentative interaction. The framework synthesizes existing approaches into coherent functional categories, validated across multiple collaborative learning tasks and communication media with strong inter-coder reliability.

ijCSCL_7_4_2.title: Interactive visual tools as triggers of collaborative reasoning in entry-level pathology
ijCSCL_7_4_2.authors: Markus Nivala & Hans Rystedt & Roger Säljö & Pauliina Kronqvist & Erno Lehtinen
ijCSCL_7_4_2.summary_haiku: Virtual microscopy enables collaborative pathology learning through multimodal referential practices. This qualitative video analysis of 15 medical student pairs examined how interactive visual tools mediate diagnostic reasoning. Students organized shared visual fields using gestures, zooming, and paced negotiations to construct joint understanding. Key strategies included framing diagnostic processes, negotiating visual evidence, and extending reasoning frames when uncertain. The study demonstrates that technology becomes constitutive of face-to-face collaboration, and understanding image production techniques proves integral to medical interpretation.

ijCSCL_10_1_2.title: The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools
ijCSCL_10_1_2.summary_ollama: This study examines how high school students assess information sources, particularly when they are products of open collaboration, and how participating in the production of information sources interacts with this understanding. The findings reveal that students use both first-order (adopting known heuristics) and second-order (reflective construction of standards) strategies to assess information sources. Participating in the production of information sources can provide learners with a concrete vantage point from which to consider the information sources they use, promoting collective cognitive responsibility and second-order learning environments.
ijCSCL_10_1_2.summary_haiku: This qualitative study examined high school students' information assessment practices while contributing to a collaborative online wiki. Through 57 interviews and classroom observations, the researcher identified two information literacy strategies: first-order strategies involving established heuristics for evaluating sources, and second-order strategies involving reflective analysis of how information is produced. Findings reveal that participating in information production enhanced students' understanding of source credibility and fostered individual responsibility for contributing accurate information to public resources.

ijCSCL_7_2_4.title: How to improve collaborative learning with video tools in the classroom? Social vs. cognitive guidance for student teams
ijCSCL_7_2_4.authors: Carmen Zahn & Karsten Krauskopf & Friedrich W. Hesse & Roy Pea
ijCSCL_7_2_4.summary_haiku: Social interaction-related guidance proved more effective than cognitive task-related guidance for student teams using video tools in collaborative history learning. In a 2×2 experimental design with 148 sixteen-year-old students, teams receiving guidance emphasizing communication norms and cooperation demonstrated superior learning outcomes in historical skills and design product quality, regardless of video tool type. Results suggest focusing instructional support on group dynamics rather than task procedures.

ijCSCL_5_1_3.title: Exploring whether students’ use of labelling depends upon the type of activity
ijCSCL_5_1_3.authors: Eva Mary Bures & Philip C. Abrami & Richard F. Schmid
ijCSCL_5_1_3.summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined whether graduate students use labeling features less frequently during structured versus unstructured online dialogue. Participants (n=37) engaged in two activities: an unstructured discussion and a HipBone Game with predetermined structure. Results showed significantly reduced label usage during the structured activity, with 62% using labels multiple times unstructured versus 46% structured. Students preferred the structured dialogue but reported mixed satisfaction with labeling. Findings suggest structured activities provide alternative scaffolding, potentially rendering labeling features redundant.

ijCSCL_4_3_4.title: Collaborative corrections with spelling control: Digital resources and peer assistance
ijCSCL_4_3_4.summary_haiku: Swedish eighth-graders collaboratively corrected spelling errors using Microsoft Word's spellchecker during English writing tasks. Through conversation analysis of video-recorded sessions, the study identified how diagnostic tools and spelling lists configured different correction practices. Students preferentially used diagnostic feedback for autonomous problem-solving before requesting peer assistance or spelling suggestions, demonstrating that underspecified software instructions created space for creative collaborative engagement and language learning.

ijCSCL_10_3_0.title: Conceptualizing the intersubjective group
ijCSCL_10_3_0.summary_haiku: Stahl argues that intersubjectivity—shared understanding through joint meaning-making—is the defining characteristic of computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL). The article proposes a paradigm shift from analyzing individual learning outcomes to examining group-level phenomena, emphasizing that collaborative learning involves increased intersubjective understanding within groups rather than aggregated individual learning. CSCL research, pedagogy, and technology should prioritize the group as the unit of analysis.

ijCSCL_6_2_1.title: Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms Carol K. K. Chan
ijCSCL_6_2_1.summary_haiku: # Summary This article examines how computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) research translates into classroom practice through a case study of knowledge-building implementation in Hong Kong schools. Using design-based research across macro (policy), meso (teacher networks), and micro (classroom) levels, the study identifies three critical themes: systemic alignment across educational levels, capacity building through principle-based teacher communities, and innovation as continuous inquiry. Findings demonstrate that sustained CSCL adoption requires coordinating institutional policies, teacher professional development networks, and classroom design while adapting research models to local socio-cultural contexts.

ijCSCL_5_3_1.title: Online moderation of synchronous e-argumentation
ijCSCL_5_3_1.authors: Christa S. C. Asterhan & Baruch B. Schwarz
ijCSCL_5_3_1.summary_haiku: This exploratory study examines effective online moderation of synchronous small-group argumentation in co-located classrooms. Through student questionnaires and protocol analyses of moderated discussions using Digalo software, researchers found that generic scaffolding prompts—effective in face-to-face settings—were ineffective in synchronous e-discussions. Instead, content-specific, involved moderation styles that disguised scaffolding as peer participation proved more effective and appreciated by students.

ijCSCL_5_4_0.title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
ijCSCL_5_4_0.summary_haiku: Stahl and Hesse critique three approaches to CSCL research, arguing that the most productive approach develops theories specifically tailored to collaborative learning's unique characteristics. They contend that CSCL requires elaborated theories addressing multiple interpenetrating levels—individual, group, classroom—and technological mediation, moving beyond folk theories and borrowed frameworks to capture phenomena distinctive to computer-supported contexts.

ijCSCL_10_4_1.title: Advancing knowledge‐building discourse through judgments of promising ideas
ijCSCL_10_4_1.authors: Bodong Chen1 & Marlene Scardamalia2 & Carl Bereiter2
ijCSCL_10_4_1.summary_haiku: Grade 3 students demonstrated capability in making promisingness judgments—evaluating ideas for their potential to advance knowledge—when supported by explicit discussion and a digital tool integrated into Knowledge Forum. Design-based research revealed students could distinguish ideas worth developing from mere facts, and promisingness judgments significantly enhanced collaborative discourse and scientific knowledge advancement compared to control classrooms.

ijCSCL_4_2_3.title: Genre and CSCL: The form and rhetoric of the online posting
ijCSCL_4_2_3.summary_haiku: This study applies genre analysis to online discussion postings in CSCL contexts, hypothesizing that educational postings share rhetorical characteristics with their epistolary precursor, the letter. Through content analysis of 136 postings, the author identifies 240 rhetorical markers reflecting epistolary dynamics, including salutations, present-tense references, and temporal references. Findings suggest that cultural and historical factors embedded in familiar genres significantly shape how students engage in online collaborative learning, beyond technological affordances alone.

ijCSCL_6_1_4.title: Exploring e-learners' perceptions of net-based peer-reviewed English writing
ijCSCL_6_1_4.summary_haiku: This study examined asynchronous, blind peer review for improving Chinese adult e-learners' English writing. Thirty-six students divided into three ability groups participated in a year-long experiment with rotating cross-group peer reviews mediated by the instructor. Results showed all groups improved, with lower-ability students making greater progress than higher-ability students. However, high-ability students became discouraged when paired with lower-ability peers for extended periods, suggesting flexible grouping strategies may be necessary.

ijCSCL_7_3_3.title: Patterns of kindergarten children’s social interaction with peers in the computer area
ijCSCL_7_3_3.summary_haiku: This qualitative study examined kindergarten children's peer interactions in a classroom computer area through three-month observations and teacher interviews. The researcher identified six social interaction patterns: parallel play, verbal conflicts, sociable interactions, knowledge construction through positive processes, knowledge construction through negative processes, and non-verbal communication. Three patterns—positive processes, negative processes, and non-verbal communication—constituted "Cognitively Effective Social Interaction" leading to meaningful knowledge construction. Findings demonstrate computers support collaborative learning when integrated with classroom curriculum.

ijCSCL_6_3_6.title: Analyzing temporal patterns of knowledge construction in a role-based online discussion
ijCSCL_6_3_6.authors: Alyssa Friend Wise & Ming Ming Chiu
ijCSCL_6_3_6.summary_haiku: This study analyzed temporal patterns of knowledge construction in role-based online discussions using content analysis and statistical discourse analysis. Examining 252 posts from 21 university students, researchers identified pivotal posts that divided discussions into distinct segments. Results showed most discussions progressed from lower to higher knowledge construction phases, with mid-discussion summaries by Synthesizer and Wrapper roles acting as pivotal posts that elevated subsequent discussion quality, supporting the progressive nature of collaborative knowledge construction.

ijCSCL_7_1_1.title: Making rounds: The routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers
ijCSCL_7_1_1.summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological study analyzes teacher interventions during collaborative computer-based learning using video recordings of English lessons with storyboarding software. Through detailed conversation analysis of naturally occurring classroom interactions, the author identifies five types of teacher practices: ratifying pupil work, reminding pupils of task requirements, making suggestions for improvement, maintaining classroom control, and making whole-class announcements. The analysis reveals that classroom management and pedagogy are intertwined rather than separate, and tensions between teacher and pupil perspectives are collaborative rather than antagonistic.

ijCSCL_7_1_0.title: Ethnomethodologically informed
ijCSCL_7_1_0.summary_haiku: Ethnomethodology (EM), founded by Harold Garfinkel, offers a research approach particularly suited to analyzing computer-supported collaborative learning by examining how people create intersubjective understanding through observable meaning-making methods. Unlike traditional educational research emphasizing individual mental states or societal forces, EM focuses on small-group interactions through sequential discourse analysis, enabling researchers to understand collaborative learning processes without imposing predetermined theoretical frameworks.

ijCSCL_6_3_7.title: The impact of scripted roles on online collaborative learning processes
ijCSCL_6_3_7.summary_haiku: This pilot study examined how scripted "opinion-centered" roles impact online collaborative learning in an asynchronous text-based environment. Using content analysis of 209 student messages and post-activity questionnaires, researchers evaluated four dimensions: participative, social, cognitive, and teaching. Results showed roles effectively fostered group cohesion and knowledge building, though metacognition remained underdeveloped. Students' perceptions largely aligned with message analysis, indicating awareness of the collaborative process.

ijCSCL_7_3_2.title: Context matters: The value of analyzing human factors within educational contexts as a way of informing technology-related decisions within design research
ijCSCL_7_3_2.summary_haiku: Design research in educational technology often overlooks systematic analysis of contextual factors. This study adapts Cognitive Work Analysis (CWA), an engineering method, to systematically identify human factors constraints—political, organizational, team, psychological, and physical—within a teacher education program. Through interviews, documentation analysis, and observations, 358 constraints were identified. The modified CWA approach made contextual information explicit and organized, enabling informed technology design decisions for supporting student research projects through an online mentorship environment.

ijCSCL_6_1_5.title: The logic of wikis: The possibilities of the Web 2.0 classroom
ijCSCL_6_1_5.summary_haiku: Web 2.0 tools like wikis and blogs can enable Dewey's vision of democratic education by supporting abductive reasoning—the logic of hypothesis generation essential for creative problem-solving. Unlike traditional deductive approaches emphasizing certainty, abduction requires simultaneously maintaining multiple competing premises, a capability previously impossible in classrooms but now feasible through hypertext-based technologies that create scale-free networks of interconnected information nodes.

ijCSCL_4_2_2.title: Affordances revisited: Articulating a Merleau-Pontian view
ijCSCL_4_2_2.summary_haiku: This article develops a Merleau-Pontian account of affordances for CSCL, arguing that existing interpretations within the field contain unresolved ontological and epistemological tensions. The author proposes that affordances are dynamic, relational, and skill-relative properties existing independently of perception but relative to agents' body-schematic interaction potential. This framework shifts design and empirical research focus toward background structuring and learners' developing capabilities rather than mental models.

ijCSCL_4_4_4.title: An ontology engineering approach to the realization of theory-driven group formation
ijCSCL_4_4_4.authors: Seiji Isotani & Akiko Inaba & Mitsuru Ikeda & Riichiro Mizoguchi
ijCSCL_4_4_4.summary_haiku: This research presents an ontology-based framework for theory-driven group formation in collaborative learning. Using ontological engineering, the authors formalize learning theory concepts to guide group composition, role assignment, and activity design. A proof-of-concept experiment with four instructors and twenty participants demonstrated that groups formed according to pedagogical theory specifications showed significantly better performance and more meaningful interactions than control groups, suggesting ontologies effectively operationalize learning theories for improved collaborative learning outcomes.

ijCSCL_10_4_0.title: A decade of CSCL
ijCSCL_10_4_0.summary_haiku: CSCL research has shifted from individual cognitive frameworks toward post-cognitive theories emphasizing group-level interaction and collaborative knowledge building. However, implementation gaps persist: technologies often reflect individual learning models, analysis methods remain cognitively focused, and widespread educational adoption remains limited. Future progress requires international collaboration, design-based research, teacher professional development, and curriculum alignment to transform global education through computer-supported collaborative learning approaches.

ijCSCL_5_4_1.title: Can the interactive whiteboard support young children’s collaborative communication and thinking in classroom science activities?
ijCSCL_5_4_1.authors: Ruth Kershner & Neil Mercer & Paul Warwick & Judith Kleine Staarman
ijCSCL_5_4_1.summary_haiku: Interactive whiteboards can support young children's collaborative communication and thinking in primary science, but effectiveness depends on multiple interacting factors. Through observational analysis of twelve classrooms, researchers found the IWB facilitates productive dialogue when combined with teacher scaffolding, established "talk rules," and appropriate classroom participation structures. However, the technology alone is not pedagogically transformative; success requires careful integration with other classroom resources and attention to both social and cognitive dimensions of collaborative learning.

ijCSCL_5_4_3.title: Using activity theory to understand intergenerational play: The case of Family Quest
ijCSCL_5_4_3.authors: Sinem Siyahhan & Sasha A. Barab & Michael P. Downton
ijCSCL_5_4_3.summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined intergenerational play between parents and children (ages 9-13) using Quest Atlantis, an educational 3D game, through activity theory analysis. Five-week observations of seven parent-child dyads revealed that successful collaborative gaming required shared intentions and expertise exchange. While outcomes varied across dyads, the research demonstrated that educational video games can facilitate meaningful family bonding and learning, particularly when designed to encourage parents and children to leverage complementary skills around personally relevant narratives.

ijCSCL_10_4_2.title: Investigating the effects of prompts on argumentation style, consensus and perceived efficacy in collaborative learning
ijCSCL_10_4_2.authors: Owen M. Harney1 & Michael J. Hogan1 & Benjamin Broome2 & Tony Hall1 & Cormac Ryan1
ijCSCL_10_4_2.summary_haiku: Process-level prompts during collaborative learning sessions significantly enhance group outcomes compared to task-level prompts. In an experimental study using Interactive Management with 75 psychology students, process-level prompts increased perceived consensus and perceived efficacy of the methodology. Analysis of group dialogue revealed more sophisticated argumentation patterns and greater complexity in consensus-based problem models among process-level groups, suggesting that facilitator prompting style substantially influences collaborative learning effectiveness.

ijCSCL_4_2_0.title: Practice perspectives in CSCL
ijCSCL_4_2_0.summary_haiku: This editorial argues that CSCL research should adopt practice perspectives to understand how collaborative learning emerges at individual, group, and community levels. Rather than studying interaction through controlled variables and statistical regularities, practice perspectives focus on how people actually interact, examining embodied and materially mediated human activity. The issue's articles demonstrate this approach by analyzing group coordination practices, technology affordances relative to user interaction potential, genre adaptation in virtual environments, and metaskills required for knowledge-creation practices.

ijCSCL_7_3_0.title: An international research community
ijCSCL_7_3_0.authors: Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse
ijCSCL_7_3_0.summary_haiku: The International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning demonstrates significant scholarly impact, ranking eleventh among education journals with a 2.243 impact factor. The journal supports a thriving international research community across fifty-three countries, publishing diverse, interdisciplinary research on collaborative learning technologies through rigorous peer review and design-based methodologies that advance CSCL theory and practice globally.

ijCSCL_5_2_5.title: Promoting metacognitive skills through peer scaffolding in a CSCL environment
ijCSCL_5_2_5.summary_haiku: A longitudinal case study of 18 university students using the KnowCat knowledge-building system over two semesters examined how peer scaffolding develops metacognitive skills in computer-supported collaborative learning. Content analysis of student annotations revealed statistically significant increases in metacognitive processes, particularly in monitoring and clarity-seeking behaviors. Results suggest pedagogical use of CSCL environments with structured peer feedback effectively enhances students' self-regulation and collaborative problem-solving capabilities.

ijCSCL_10_2_4.title: An integrated way of using a tangible user interface in a classroom
ijCSCL_10_2_4.authors: Sebastien Cuendet & Jessica Dehler-Zufferey & Giulia Ortoleva & Pierre Dillenbourg
ijCSCL_10_2_4.summary_haiku: Researchers designed a classroom activity using TapaCarp, a tangible user interface, to teach carpenter apprentices spatial skills while bridging school and workplace learning. The mixed-methods study with 40 apprentices across three classes showed high usability and strong engagement, with improved artifact quality from day one to day two. However, standardized tests revealed no significant learning gains compared to controls, though plausible objects proved more effective than non-plausible ones for complex tasks.

ijCSCL_7_1_2.title: How gamers manage aggression: Situating skills in collaborative computer games
ijCSCL_7_1_2.authors: Ulrika Bennerstedt & Jonas Ivarsson & Jonas Linderoth
ijCSCL_7_1_2.summary_haiku: Using ethnomethodological analysis of boss encounters in a massively multiplayer online game, this study examines skills gamers develop during collaborative gameplay involving portrayed aggression. The researchers found that "aggression" and "collaboration" manifest as highly specialized, game-specific practices—particularly aggro management—rather than transferable general skills. The analysis challenges assumptions underlying both positive and negative gaming effects research, arguing that claims about behavioral transfer require explicit theoretical justification and risk oversimplification.

ijCSCL_6_3_5.title: Are two heads always better than one? Differential effects of collaboration on students’ computer-supported learning in mathematics
ijCSCL_6_3_5.authors: Dejana Mullins & Nikol Rummel & Hans Spada
ijCSCL_6_3_5.summary_haiku: Collaboration's effectiveness in mathematics learning depends on instructional material type. This experimental study compared individual versus collaborative learning with conceptual and procedural algebra instruction in a computer-supported environment. Results showed collaboration enhanced conceptual knowledge acquisition through mutual elaboration, but hindered procedural skill development due to task distribution and reduced practice opportunities.

ijCSCL_6_3_4.title: Scaffolding collaborative technical writing with procedural facilitation and synchronous discussion
ijCSCL_6_3_4.authors: Shiou-Wen Yeh & Jia-Jiunn Lo & Jeng-Jia Huang
ijCSCL_6_3_4.summary_haiku: Researchers developed Process-Writing Wizard, a computer-supported system combining procedural scaffolding and synchronous chat to facilitate collaborative technical writing among EFL students. An experimental study with 48 students compared the system against standard chat. Results showed experimental group students demonstrated significantly higher perceived usefulness, positive attitudes, and stronger intention to reuse the system. Their articles exhibited superior content and organization quality, and synchronous discussions focused more on article-related interactions rather than social exchanges.

ijCSCL_7_1_3.title: The multivoicedness of game play: Exploring the unfolding of a student’s learning trajectory in a gaming context at school
ijCSCL_7_1_3.summary_haiku: This qualitative case study examines how classroom interactions facilitate a student's learning trajectory while playing the educational game Global Conflicts: Palestine. Using sociocultural and dialogic analysis of video-recorded gameplay and discussions, the research demonstrates that computer games become learning resources through collaborative meaning-making. The teacher's role in orchestrating dialogic spaces where multiple perspectives "inter-animate" each other proved crucial for developing nuanced understanding of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict's complexity.

ijCSCL_5_2_4.title: Distributed leadership in online groups
ijCSCL_5_2_4.summary_haiku: In an asynchronous online learning environment, pre-service teachers working in small groups demonstrated highly distributed leadership across all members, with different leadership forms showing varying distribution patterns. While successful group performance was not directly predicted by overall leadership distribution patterns, qualitative analysis revealed that effective groups developed internal organizational structures and positive interpersonal dynamics that facilitated both peer and instructor engagement, suggesting emergent distributed leadership offers a viable alternative to scripted collaborative roles.

ijCSCL_6_1_6.title: Perspective taking and synchronous argumentation for learning the day/night cycle
ijCSCL_6_1_6.authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Yaron Schur & Haim Pensso & Naama Tayer
ijCSCL_6_1_6.summary_haiku: Combining perspective-taking through pictures and synchronous computer-supported argumentation promotes conceptual learning of the day/night cycle in Grade 8 students. Using the Digalo tool and design-research methodology with pre-post testing, the study found significant improvements in mental models, elaboration, and knowledge integration. However, teacher mediation during small-group discussions did not enhance learning outcomes, suggesting that meticulous task design and peer argumentation were primary drivers of conceptual change.

ijCSCL_7_3_1.title: Learning physics through play in an augmented reality environment
ijCSCL_7_3_1.authors: Noel Enyedy & Joshua A. Danish & Girlie Delacruz & Melissa Kumar
ijCSCL_7_3_1.summary_haiku: # Summary This study demonstrates that first and second graders (n=43) can meaningfully learn Newtonian physics through augmented reality activities combining embodied play and progressive symbolization. Using pre-post assessments, students showed significant gains in understanding force, net force, friction, and two-dimensional motion. Two design principles guided the curriculum: participatory modeling leveraging socio-dramatic play to make intuitions visible, and progressive symbolization enabling students to invent and refine representational systems. Case studies illustrate how embodied prediction and collaborative symbol refinement supported conceptual integration, though challenges emerged when students relied exclusively on embodiment or formal reasoning.

ijCSCL_4_2_1.title: The joint organization of interaction within a multimodal CSCL medium
ijCSCL_4_2_1.authors: Murat Perit Çakır & Alan Zemel & Gerry Stahl
ijCSCL_4_2_1.summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological case study examines how three students organize collaborative mathematical problem-solving in a synchronous dual-interaction online environment combining text chat and shared whiteboard. Through sequential interaction analysis, the authors reveal that students co-construct shared mathematical understanding by coordinating visual, narrative, and symbolic representations across media. The indexical field formed by referential links between chat messages and whiteboard drawings establishes common ground, enabling group cognition and deep mathematical learning through multiple realizations of mathematical objects.

ijCSCL_10_4_3.title: ReaderBench: Automated evaluation of collaboration based on cohesion and dialogism
ijCSCL_10_4_3.authors: Mihai Dascalu1 & Stefan Trausan-Matu1 & Danielle S. McNamara2 & Philippe Dessus3
ijCSCL_10_4_3.summary_haiku: ReaderBench proposes two computational models for automated collaboration assessment in CSCL conversations. The dialogical voice inter-animation model evaluates collaboration through overlapping semantic chains representing different participants' viewpoints, while the social knowledge-building model analyzes longitudinal cohesion patterns. Validation against human annotations of ten chat conversations demonstrates both models reliably identify collaboration zones and predict overall collaboration quality, supporting cohesion and voice inter-animation as collaboration signatures.

ijCSCL_5_4_2.title: Sharing and cultivating tacit knowledge in an online learning environment
ijCSCL_5_4_2.summary_haiku: Online graduate business students cultivated tacit knowledge through a strategic management course using naturalistic inquiry methodology. The course combined readings, threaded discussions, and a simulation game, creating a "ba" (shared context) that encouraged socialization, externalization, combination, and internalization processes aligned with Nonaka's knowledge creation model. Students reported learning tacit dimensions impossible to acquire from textbooks alone.

ijCSCL_4_4_3.title: Contrasting the use of tools for presentation and critique: Some cases from architectural education
ijCSCL_4_4_3.authors: Gustav Lymer & Jonas Ivarsson & Oskar Lindwall
ijCSCL_4_4_3.summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological video analysis of architectural design reviews examines how presentation technologies shape critique practices. Comparing poster-based, digital slideshow, and hybrid setups across 143 sessions, the study reveals that digital technologies fundamentally transform sequential organization, shared attention, and part-whole relations during discussion and assessment. The findings suggest that presentation tools designed primarily for delivery may inadequately support subsequent critique, highlighting the need for spatially organized interfaces better suited to collaborative design review practices.

ijCSCL_4_2_5.title: A knowledge-practice perspective on technology-mediated learning
ijCSCL_4_2_5.summary_haiku: Technology enhances learning through transformed social practices, not merely through tool implementation. While knowledge-building theory emphasizes idea advancement, this perspective argues that genuine educational transformation requires cultivating epistemic practices—socially embedded ways of working with knowledge—that channel intellectual efforts toward collective knowledge advancement. Material artifacts and social practices constitute dialectical unity in knowledge creation.

ijCSCL_7_3_5.title: 4SPPIces: A case study of factors in a scripted collaborative-learning blended course across spatial locations
ijCSCL_7_3_5.authors: Mar Pérez-Sanagustín & Patricia Santos & Davinia Hernández-Leo & Josep Blat
ijCSCL_7_3_5.summary_haiku: This case study evaluates the 4SPPIces model—a conceptual framework combining Space, Pedagogical Method, Participants, and History factors—for designing computer-supported collaborative blended learning scripts. Researchers implemented a geography fieldwork activity with 34 students across Barcelona using mobile devices and GPS. Results demonstrate that considering 4SPPIces factors successfully enhanced the activity, promoting collaborative skills, motivation, and learning about multiple urban districts while effectively supporting teacher orchestration through integrated technologies.

ijCSCL_6_1_2.title: Temporality matters: Advancing a method for analyzing problem-solving processes in a computer-supported collaborative environment
ijCSCL_6_1_2.summary_haiku: This study advances Lag-sequential Analysis (LsA) as a quantitative method for examining temporal patterns in computer-supported collaborative learning groups. Applied to synchronous online problem-solving discussions, LsA revealed significant sequential interaction patterns invisible to traditional "coding and counting" approaches. Critically, temporal transition patterns between process categories emerged as the strongest predictor of group performance, demonstrating that analyzing the order and sequence of collaborative interactions—not merely their frequency—is essential for understanding collaborative learning processes.

ijCSCL_5_2_0.title: A prism of CSCL research
ijCSCL_5_2_0.summary_haiku: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning integrates diverse disciplines, technologies, and methodologies to study collaborative learning with digital tools. This issue presents five empirical studies examining different CSCL applications—from complex system simulations to scripted collaboration platforms—using varied analytical approaches including classroom assessments, discourse analysis, and quantitative-qualitative combinations. The research demonstrates that effective CSCL design requires attention to pedagogical aims and collaborative processes rather than relying on single technological solutions.

ijCSCL_7_1_7.title: The role of teacher assistance on the effects of a macro-script in collaborative writing tasks
ijCSCL_7_1_7.summary_haiku: This multiple-case study examines how teacher assistance patterns interact with macro-scripts to influence collaborative writing in university students. Analyzing two settings with different script types and teaching approaches, the study identifies distinct teacher assistance patterns and their relationships to group organization and knowledge construction phases. Results show that flexible, content-focused teacher guidance combined with open scripts promotes heterogeneous group strategies and advanced collaborative knowledge construction, while detailed scripts paired with organizational reminders produce homogeneous adherence but lower knowledge construction levels.

ijCSCL_6_3_0.title: Tweets from #cscl2011
ijCSCL_6_3_0.authors: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich W. Hesse & Nancy Law
ijCSCL_6_3_0.summary_haiku: # Summary The CSCL 2011 conference in Hong Kong demonstrated significant growth in computer-supported collaborative learning research, particularly in Asia-Pacific regions, with over 400 participants from 30+ countries. The conference emphasized connecting CSCL research to educational policy and practice through keynotes, workshops, and post-conference events across Chinese cities, establishing CSCL as a vital research field globally.

ijCSCL_10_2_1.title: The impact of hierarchical positions on communities of learning
ijCSCL_10_2_1.authors: Martin Rehm & Wim Gijselaers & Mien Segers
ijCSCL_10_2_1.summary_haiku: Hierarchical positions significantly influence participants' activity and performance in online Communities of Learning within organizations.
