Analyzing 249 staff members across 25 CoLs, this empirical study found that higher-ranked employees contributed more frequently and achieved better exam grades. However, cluster analysis revealed a "Stars" group of exceptional performers transcending hierarchical constraints, suggesting that while organizational hierarchy shapes collaborative behavior, individual motivation can overcome these structural barriers.

ijCSCL_10_2_0.title: The core features of CSCL: Social situation, collaborative knowledge processes and their design
ijCSCL_10_2_0.summary_haiku: This editorial examines three core CSCL features: how social situations influence collaboration, the nature of collaborative knowledge processes, and effective design of learning environments. Through analyzing four empirical studies across diverse contexts, the authors identify that social awareness significantly impacts learning outcomes, knowledge creation remains rare despite ideal conditions, and technical tools combined with thoughtful orchestration can enhance collaborative learning, though predicting emergent group cognition remains challenging.

ijCSCL_6_3_1.title: Student use of Facebook for organizing collaborative classroom activities
ijCSCL_6_3_1.authors: Cliff Lampe & Donghee Yvette Wohn & Jessica Vitak & Nicole B. Ellison & Rick Wash
ijCSCL_6_3_1.summary_haiku: Two survey studies examined how undergraduate students repurpose Facebook for classroom organizing. Study 1 (N=302) found that Facebook intensity and willingness to contact instructors predicted collaboration propensity. Study 2 (N=214) revealed two distinct collaboration types: positive (instructor-approved) and negative (unapproved), with different predictors including self-efficacy and relational communication strategies, suggesting how students use Facebook matters more than frequency.

ijCSCL_7_1_6.title: Linking teacher beliefs, practices and student inquiry-based learning in a CSCL environment: A tale of two teachers
ijCSCL_7_1_6.summary_haiku: Teachers holding innovation-oriented beliefs about inquiry-based learning enacted mathematics lessons with inquiry principle-based practices and technology-enhanced orchestration, while teachers with teacher-centered beliefs used traditional approaches. Comparative case analysis of two teachers using Group Scribbles technology revealed that innovation-oriented beliefs directly shaped progressive inquiry practices, which subsequently fostered student collaborative knowledge construction and effective technology use.

ijCSCL_5_2_1.title: Mr. Vetro: A Collective Simulation for teaching health science
ijCSCL_5_2_1.authors: Andri Ioannidou & Alexander Repenning & David Webb & Diane Keyser & Lisa Luhn & Christof Daetwyler
ijCSCL_5_2_1.summary_haiku: Mr. Vetro is a collective simulation where students collaboratively control physiological organs on networked computers to learn about system interactions. Formal evaluation across 400 high school students demonstrated significant learning gains in physiological knowledge and vocabulary, increased inquiry-based teaching practices, and positive real-life health behavior changes, though attitudes toward science remained relatively stable.

ijCSCL_6_1_3.title: Learning the physics of electricity: A qualitative analysis of collaborative processes involved in productive failure
ijCSCL_6_1_3.authors: Suneeta A. Pathak & Beaumie Kim & Michael J. Jacobson & Baohui Zhang
ijCSCL_6_1_3.summary_haiku: This qualitative study examines collaborative problem-solving dynamics in physics education using computer-supported learning. Two student dyads—one experiencing productive failure through initial low-structured activities followed by high-structured ones, and another receiving only high-structured activities—solved electricity problems using NetLogo models. Analysis of video, screen captures, and solutions revealed that initial struggle enabled deeper engagement with the model and reflective reasoning, while over-scripted activities hindered meaningful collaboration and conceptual understanding.

ijCSCL_7_3_4.title: Online class size, note reading, note writing and collaborative discourse
ijCSCL_7_3_4.authors: Mingzhu Qiu & Jim Hewitt & Clare Brett
ijCSCL_7_3_4.summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined 25 online graduate courses (341 students, 25 instructors) using tracking logs and interviews to investigate how class size affects note reading and writing loads. Findings revealed class size positively correlates with total notes read but negatively with percentage read, indicating information overload in larger classes. Students wrote shorter, simpler notes in larger classes. Dividing large classes into subgroups reduced overload. An optimal class size of 13-15 students was identified for effective collaborative discourse.

ijCSCL_4_2_4.title: Exploring metaskills of knowledge-creating inquiry in higher education
ijCSCL_4_2_4.summary_haiku: This study investigates metaskills required for knowledge-creating inquiry in higher education through an 11-week undergraduate psychology course using progressive inquiry and web-based collaboration. Qualitative analysis of database discourse and student self-reflections revealed three student groups exhibited varying engagement levels in collaborative object-oriented inquiry. Group C demonstrated superior skills in monitoring individual, collective, and object-oriented aspects of inquiry, while Groups A and B struggled with shared knowledge advancement. Findings suggest metaskills for collaborative knowledge creation develop through sustained socialization into inquiry practices emphasizing iterative development of shared epistemic objects.

ijCSCL_4_4_2.title: Earth science learning in SMALLab: A design experiment for mixed reality
ijCSCL_4_4_2.summary_haiku: This design experiment examined how mixed-reality environments support collaborative earth science learning. Researchers implemented SMALLab, a semi-immersive platform enabling colocated students to interact face-to-face within computationally mediated spaces. A 3-day intervention with 72 high school students revealed significantly increased student-to-student exchanges compared to traditional instruction and notable achievement gains on concept assessments, suggesting mixed-reality technology's potential for enhancing K-12 collaborative learning when properly designed.

ijCSCL_10_4_4.title: AMOEBA: Designing for collaboration in computer science classrooms through live learning analytics
ijCSCL_10_4_4.authors: Matthew Berland1 & Don Davis2 & Carmen Petrick Smith3
ijCSCL_10_4_4.summary_haiku: AMOEBA is a learning analytics tool designed to support teachers in orchestrating real-time collaboration among novice programmers using the IPRO visual programming environment. The study examined how pairing students based on a "surprising similarity" metric—operationalizing Zone of Proximal Development for computer science—affected programming outcomes across eight classes. Results showed that paired students produced programs with greater complexity, depth, and novelty compared to unpaired work, with improvements persisting after pairing ended.

ijCSCL_4_4_0.title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
ijCSCL_4_4_0.summary_haiku: This article identifies four theoretical paradigms for understanding shared knowledge in computer-supported collaborative learning: sharing individual mental representations, sharing an object, sharing a situation, and sharing a community. The authors argue that researchers' implicit or explicit adoption of these paradigms significantly influences educational intervention design and effectiveness, regardless of whether designers consciously recognize their theoretical assumptions about knowledge sharing.

ijCSCL_6_1_1.title: The Singapore experience: Synergy of national policy, classroom practice and design research
ijCSCL_6_1_1.authors: Chee-Kit Looi & Hyo-Jeong So & Yancy Toh & Wenli Chen
ijCSCL_6_1_1.summary_haiku: Singapore's systemic approach to CSCL integration demonstrates how design research methodology bridges macro-level policy, meso-level school implementation, and micro-level classroom interactions. Through the GroupScribbles project across multiple schools, researchers co-designed collaborative learning activities with teachers, developed design principles for rapid collaborative knowledge improvement, and achieved sustainable adoption. This multi-level alignment of policy, practice, and research provides a model for scaling CSCL innovations while addressing real classroom constraints.

ijCSCL_5_2_3.title: Scripting a distance-learning university course: Do students benefit from net-based scripted collaboration?
ijCSCL_5_2_3.summary_haiku: This experimental field study examined whether scripted collaboration benefits net-based learning in a semester-long university operating systems course. Forty-two student groups performed brainstorming, clustering, and essay-writing tasks either with system-enforced scripts or non-scripted instructions. Results showed no general advantage of scripting for knowledge acquisition or task performance. However, principal component analysis revealed scripting slightly improved essay coherence and comprehensibility, suggesting benefits for complex tasks requiring deeper understanding.

ijCSCL_6_3_3.title: Agent-based dynamic support for learning from collaborative brainstorming in scientific inquiry
ijCSCL_6_3_3.authors: Hao-Chuan Wang & Carolyn P. Rosé & Chun-Yen Chang
ijCSCL_6_3_3.summary_haiku: This study examines learning during collaborative brainstorming through two controlled experiments manipulating individual versus pair work and system support. Results reveal that while pair brainstorming produces process losses in idea generation, it enhances multi-perspective learning. The VIBRANT agent's automatic feedback improves connection-based learning. An enhanced version in study two shows promise for mitigating productivity losses associated with collaborative work.

ijCSCL_7_1_4.title: Personal and shared experiences as resources for meaning making in a philosophy of science course
ijCSCL_7_1_4.summary_haiku: Health education students in an online philosophy of science course used personal work experiences and peer contributions as meaning-making resources. Analysis of individual writings and discussions revealed three epistemic activities: applying theoretical concepts to practice, forming conceptions, and critiquing. Peer interactions involved elaboration and sharing discourse. Results demonstrate that connecting abstract philosophical knowledge to lived experience enhanced understanding while fostering boundary crossing between institutional and personal knowledge contexts.

ijCSCL_10_2_2.title: Peer interaction and social network analysis of online communities with the support of awareness of different contexts
ijCSCL_10_2_2.authors: Jian-Wei Lin1 & Li-Jung Mai2 & Yung-Cheng Lai1
ijCSCL_10_2_2.summary_haiku: This study directly compares social-context awareness (SA) and knowledge-context awareness (KA) in online learning communities using identical experimental settings. Through a semester-long investigation with repeated measurements, researchers found that SA stimulated significantly more quantitative peer interaction than KA, particularly in later stages. However, both approaches had limited capacity to enhance message quality. Despite similar midterm performance, the SA community demonstrated significantly better learning outcomes on the final posttest, likely attributed to more extensive peer interaction patterns.

ijCSCL_10_2_3.title: Fixed group and opportunistic collaboration in a CSCL environment
ijCSCL_10_2_3.authors: Tuya Siqin & Jan van Aalst & Samuel Kai Wah Chu
ijCSCL_10_2_3.summary_haiku: This study examined 27 Chinese undergraduates' synchronous online discourse across two phases: fixed group collaboration (8 weeks) and opportunistic collaboration (8 weeks) using Knowledge Forum. Multi-faceted analysis revealed that while all groups showed similar interaction patterns, productive groups generated higher-level questions and ideas. Opportunistic collaboration enabled broader interactions and more constructive discourse but exhibited scattered interactions and reduced metacognition. Active participation and high-level idea contributions correlated positively with domain knowledge gains.

ijCSCL_7_1_5.title: Collaboration amidst disagreement and moral judgment: The dynamics of Jewish and Arab students’ collaborative inquiry of their joint past
ijCSCL_7_1_5.summary_haiku: Israeli Jewish and Arab students collaboratively investigated a historical event through computer-supported learning, analyzing conflicting narratives via wiki-based discussion. Despite persistent disagreement, students' post-activity individual answers demonstrated enriched historical understanding, incorporating multiple perspectives and reduced one-sidedness. The researchers propose "fission"—moments when opposing voices create cracks in individual perspectives, fostering polyphonic thinking without requiring consensus.

ijCSCL_6_3_2.title: Identity presence and knowledge building: Joint emergence in online learning environments?
ijCSCL_6_3_2.authors: Fengfeng Ke & Alicia F. Chávez & Pei-Ni L. Causarano & Antonio Causarano
ijCSCL_6_3_2.summary_haiku: This mixed-method study examined identity presence in seven online courses and its relationship to knowledge building. Using discourse analysis of 1,817 discussion posts, researchers found that posts expressing personal experiences, cultural perspectives, and age-related views elicited significantly more responses and correlated with knowledge-sharing interactions. However, identity presence did not significantly predict higher-level collaborative knowledge construction, suggesting online learners prioritize self-expression over negotiating shared understanding.

ijCSCL_5_2_2.title: Animation and grammar in science education: Learners’ construal of animated educational software Göran Karlsson
ijCSCL_5_2_2.summary_haiku: This case study examines how two upper-secondary students collaboratively interpret animated biochemical processes through written reports. Using interaction analysis of video-recorded sessions, the research reveals that students' grammatically constructed narratives prioritize perceptually salient animated features as active subjects, deriving noun phrases from animation and educational text while substituting verbs with everyday language. Without sufficient subject-matter knowledge, students cannot evaluate adequacy and rely solely on grammatical correctness, resulting in non-scientific explanations. The findings emphasize that technology-supported science education requires consideration of both cultural and semiotic processes.

ijCSCL_6_1_0.title: CSCL in Asia
ijCSCL_6_1_0.summary_haiku: Asian countries are achieving superior educational outcomes through forward-looking policies emphasizing collaborative knowledge building and twenty-first-century skills rather than rote learning. This editorial examines CSCL research and implementation across Asia, highlighting Singapore's multi-level reform approach integrating micro, meso, and macro educational scales, and presenting empirical studies on productive failure, peer review, and inquiry-based learning from Asian contexts.

ijCSCL_4_4_1.title: Wikis to support the “collaborative” part of collaborative learning
ijCSCL_4_4_1.summary_haiku: Wikis provide an effective platform for supporting asynchronous, non-collocated collaborative learning when enhanced with awareness, navigation, and communication components. Two case studies demonstrate that prefabricated wiki structures function as coordinating representations, enabling both tightly coupled team design projects and loosely coupled co-blogging activities to maintain adequate intersubjective spaces for productive student collaboration.

ijCSCL_5_4_4.title: The collaborative construction of chronotopes during computer-supported collaborative professional tasks
ijCSCL_5_4_4.summary_haiku: # Summary This study analyzes how teachers collaboratively construct spatial and temporal frameworks during computer-supported professional planning using qualitative video analysis of six sessions. The researchers identified three distinct chronotopes—Adagio, Andante, and Allegretto—representing different interaction tempos shaped by tool features, activity complexity, and participant expertise. Results demonstrate that technology mediates collaboration by creating multiple overlapping spaces where different types of coordination emerge, revealing how space-time co-construction fundamentally influences group professional work.

ijCSCL_8_4_2.title: Social argumentation in online synchronous communication
ijCSCL_8_4_2.summary_haiku: This study examined argumentative practices among adolescents in World of Warcraft synchronous guild chat using ethnographic methods. Analysis of 27 argumentative exchanges revealed that 81% employed counter-critiques—stronger arguments directly refuting opponents' claims—rather than weaker counter-alternatives. Quality argumentation peaked during discussions about avatar customization (race/class, gear, talent builds), suggesting that interest-driven, authentic contexts where players exercise control over personalization trigger sophisticated argumentative discourse skills.

ijCSCL_3_3_2.title: Context-oriented communication and the design of computer-supported discursive learning
ijCSCL_3_3_2.summary_haiku: This theory-driven design experiment develops a context-oriented communication model to guide computer-supported discursive learning (CSDL) system design. Through iterative testing of the KOLUMBUS prototype across five classroom settings, researchers identified that integrating communicative annotations directly with segmented learning material as context significantly enhances mutual understanding in asynchronous discussions. The study extends traditional dyadic communication models by introducing the facilitator as a crucial third party, providing practical design guidelines emphasizing context integration, metadata support, and facilitation features.

ijCSCL_2_1_5.title: Barriers to online critical discourse
ijCSCL_2_1_5.summary_haiku: This qualitative case study examined barriers to critical discourse in online forums within a 15-week graduate humanities course. Through observation and interviews with five distance students, researchers identified three key obstacles: students held competing orientations toward the conference (some seeking critique, others socioemotional support), perceived critiques as personal attacks, and viewed critical discourse as burdensome for participation marks. Structured learning activities with defined roles and assessment methods reflecting engagement effort could mitigate these barriers.

ijCSCL_3_1_0.title: The many levels of CSCL
ijCSCL_3_1_0.summary_haiku: CSCL research operates across multiple interconnected social levels—individual, small group, and classroom—requiring integrated pedagogical designs that coordinate activities across these levels. Effective collaborative learning depends on understanding how constraints at institutional, domain, and technological levels intersect with group dynamics, necessitating both qualitative and quantitative multilevel analyses.

ijCSCL_1_4_1.title: From dialogue to monologue and back: Middle spaces in computer-mediated learning
ijCSCL_1_4_1.summary_haiku: This study develops a framework distinguishing communication interfaces supporting dialogue from information interfaces supporting monologue in computer-mediated learning. Through design-based research with the Knowledge Integration Environment, the authors examine how students transition between these modes using SpeakEasy and SenseMaker tools. Case analyses reveal that successful learners strategically moved between dialogue and monologue, reflecting on ideas and identifying knowledge gaps, while less successful learners failed to leverage these transitions, suggesting that "middle spaces" bridging both modes enhance learning trajectories.

ijCSCL_9_2_1.title: PolyCAFe—automatic support for the polyphonic analysis of CSCL chats
ijCSCL_9_2_1.authors: Stefan Trausan-Matu & Mihai Dascalu & Traian Rebedea
ijCSCL_9_2_1.summary_haiku: PolyCAFe applies the polyphonic framework—grounded in Bakhtin's dialogism and musical metaphor—to automatically analyze collaborative learning chats. Using Natural Language Processing and Social Network Analysis, the system identifies implicit links between utterances, detects voices and their inter-animations, and generates quantitative metrics for collaboration assessment. Evaluation experiments demonstrate that PolyCAFe significantly reduces tutor feedback preparation time while providing useful insights to learners about their participation.

ijCSCL_8_2_4.title: Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation
ijCSCL_8_2_4.authors: Gahgene Gweon & Mahaveer Jain & John McDonough & Bhiksha Raj & Carolyn P. Rosé
ijCSCL_8_2_4.summary_haiku: Researchers developed an unsupervised Dynamic Bayesian Network model grounded in Speech Accommodation Theory to automatically detect other-oriented transactive contributions in dyadic speech discussions. Testing on debate recordings, they found significant positive correlation between automatic speech style accommodation measures and prevalence of other-oriented transacts (R=.36, p<.05), demonstrating that theoretically-informed computational models effectively assess collaborative learning processes.

ijCSCL_1_4_0.title: Social practices of
ijCSCL_1_4_0.summary_haiku: Computer-supported collaborative learning requires students to develop effective social practices to compensate for missing nonverbal cues in virtual environments. This editorial examines four empirical studies investigating how groups establish interaction patterns for dialogue, mathematical inquiry, blended learning dynamics, and consistent communication practices, demonstrating that social practices are central to both individual and collaborative cognition.

ijCSCL_9_2_0.title: Dialogic foundations of CSCL
ijCSCL_9_2_0.authors: Gerry Stahl & Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen & Nancy Law
ijCSCL_9_2_0.summary_haiku: Dialogical theory, rooted in Vygotsky and Bakhtin's work, provides essential foundations for CSCL by emphasizing that cognition and meaning-making emerge through social interaction rather than individual minds. This editorial examines four empirical studies employing different methodologies—from dialogical discourse analysis to controlled experiments—demonstrating that CSCL research thrives through complementary theoretical and methodological approaches to understanding collaborative learning processes.

ijCSCL_3_1_1.title: The mechanics of CSCL macro scripts
ijCSCL_3_1_1.summary_haiku: Macro scripts structure collaborative learning by strategically distributing resources, roles, and knowledge among team members to increase interaction intensity. Using pedagogical design principles and computational data structure transformations, scripts trigger knowledge-productive interactions like argumentation and explanation. The SWISH model demonstrates how scripts engineer productive learning by creating controlled "splits" that require students to interact intensively to reach shared understanding.

ijCSCL_1_2_6.title: ERRATUM Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building
ijCSCL_1_2_6.authors: Eddy Y.C. Lee & Carol K.K. Chan & Jan van Aalst
ijCSCL_1_2_6.summary_haiku: This study examined how knowledge-building portfolios and principles scaffold collaborative inquiry in computer forums. Using a quasi-experimental design with 119 ninth-grade students across three Knowledge Forum conditions, researchers found that students guided by knowledge-building principles demonstrated deeper inquiry, more high-level questions, and superior conceptual understanding compared to peers using forums alone or with portfolios only. Portfolio scores predicted domain understanding beyond individual participation measures, suggesting portfolios effectively characterize and foster collective knowledge advances.

ijCSCL_2_1_4.title: Investigating patterns of interaction in networked learning and
ijCSCL_2_1_4.authors: Maarten de Laat & Vic Lally & Lasse Lipponen & Robert-Jan Simons
ijCSCL_2_1_4.summary_haiku: Social Network Analysis (SNA) combined with content analysis and critical event recall provides valuable insights into networked learning communities. This multi-method study examined interaction patterns in an online master's program, revealing how participant roles and network density evolve over time. SNA effectively visualizes collaboration structures and identifies central versus peripheral members, complementing traditional qualitative methods to deepen understanding of computer-supported collaborative learning dynamics.

ijCSCL_3_3_3.title: Cultural practices in networked classroom learning environments
ijCSCL_3_3_3.summary_haiku: Networked classroom simulations enable underserved secondary mathematics students to leverage cultural practices as learning resources. This case study examined the Gridlock Participatory Simulation, analyzing how coordination and co-construction activities—supported by multiple communication modes including informal language, gesture, and graphical representations—invited students to draw on community-based interaction patterns while engaging in rigorous mathematical discourse and practice.

ijCSCL_8_4_3.title: Collaborative drawing on a shared digital canvas in elementary science education: The effects of script and task awareness support
ijCSCL_8_4_3.authors: Hannie Gijlers & Armin Weinberger & Alieke Mattia van Dijk & Lars Bollen & Wouter van Joolingen
ijCSCL_8_4_3.summary_haiku: This study examined how scripting and task awareness support affect elementary students' collaborative drawing on photosynthesis. Ninety-four fifth-graders worked in dyads using a shared digital canvas under three conditions: control, awareness prompts, or structured script. Both support types increased transactive discourse and deeper conceptual understanding compared to controls. Scripted students acquired significantly more conceptual knowledge, while awareness and scripting both facilitated integrative consensus-building and process-related discussions.

ijCSCL_8_4_1.title: Real-time mutual gaze perception enhances collaborative learning and collaboration quality
ijCSCL_8_4_1.summary_haiku: Real-time gaze visualization during remote collaborative learning on neuroscience contrasting cases enhanced learning gains and collaboration quality compared to control conditions. Eye-tracking enabled dyads to achieve higher joint attention, with followers benefiting most. Joint attention emerged as the primary mediator of improved learning outcomes.

ijCSCL_3_3_1.title: Analyzing collaborative learning processes automatically: Exploiting the advances of computational linguistics in
ijCSCL_3_3_1.authors: Carolyn Rosé & Yi-Chia Wang & Yue Cui & Jaime Arguello & Karsten Stegmann & Armin Weinberger & Frank Fischer
ijCSCL_3_3_1.summary_haiku: Researchers applied computational linguistics text classification technology to automatically analyze collaborative learning discourse using a multi-dimensional coding scheme. Testing on 1,250 coded segments, they achieved acceptable reliability (Kappa ≥0.7) on several dimensions by designing linguistically-informed features reflecting thread structure and discourse context, demonstrating that feature engineering proved more effective than sophisticated algorithms for this task.

ijCSCL_9_4_4.title: “I guess my question is”: What is the co-occurrence of uncertainty and learning in computer-mediated discourse?
ijCSCL_9_4_4.authors: Michelle E. Jordan & An-Chih Janne Cheng & Diane Schallert & Kwangok Song & SoonAh Lee & Yangjoo Park
ijCSCL_9_4_4.summary_haiku: This study examined how uncertainty expressions and learning co-occur in graduate students' computer-mediated discussions. Using inductive coding of 1,048 comments across synchronous and asynchronous online discussions, researchers found that 72% of paragraphs containing uncertainty also exhibited learning markers. Direct uncertainty expressions correlated with presenting new ideas and applications, while indirect expressions associated more with elaboration. Results suggest uncertainty expression facilitates productive learning through collaborative meaning-making in online environments.

ijCSCL_1_2_4.title: Knowledge-building activity structures in Japanese elementary science pedagogy
ijCSCL_1_2_4.authors: Jun Oshima & Ritsuko Oshima & Isao Murayama & Shigenori Inagaki & Makiko Takenaka & Tomokazu Yamamoto & Etsuji Yamaguchi & Hayashi Nakayama
ijCSCL_1_2_4.summary_haiku: # Summary This design study examined how to transform Japanese elementary science classrooms into knowledge-building communities by integrating traditional activity structures with CSCL technology. Across two consecutive years, researchers refined lesson designs using Knowledge Forum to support idea-centered, collaborative inquiry. Results showed that improving task authenticity and participatory structures—particularly blending online and offline communication—significantly enhanced students' collective knowledge advancement and engagement with conceptual artifacts compared to initial implementations.

ijCSCL_3_1_3.title: A Community of Practice among tutors enabling student participation in a seminar preparation
ijCSCL_3_1_3.summary_haiku: A tutor community of practice overcame institutional barriers to implementing computer-supported collaborative learning in a Computer and Law seminar. Through informal collaboration and shared identity, tutors self-organized to design and conduct an educational experiment using JurMOO, a text-based virtual platform, for seminar preparation. This bottom-up approach enabled student participation and learning where top-down professor coordination had failed, demonstrating that tutor communities can effectively support educational innovation.

ijCSCL_9_2_2.title: Disengaged students and dialogic learning: the role of CSCL affordances
ijCSCL_9_2_2.summary_haiku: This study examines how three disengaged eighth-grade students gradually adopted dialogic norms through participation in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) discussions using the Argunaut tool. Through temporal analysis of philosophical discussions, the research demonstrates that peer-mediated exposure to dialogic practices—rather than direct teacher intervention—enabled students to develop multivoicedness and expand their discursive repertoires. CSCL affordances, including delayed responses and reduced prosodic cues, facilitated this transformation.

ijCSCL_1_4_2.title: Knowledge building in mathematics: Supporting collaborative learning in pattern problems
ijCSCL_1_4_2.summary_haiku: Grade 4 students using Knowledge Forum, a collaborative online platform, demonstrated sophisticated mathematical reasoning when solving pattern generalization problems. Students found multiple algebraic rules per problem, revised their conjectures over weeks, and increasingly provided detailed justifications—behaviors rarely observed in traditional instruction. Knowledge-building principles of epistemic agency and idea improvement fostered this inquiry orientation, with students spontaneously recognizing structural similarities across problems.

ijCSCL_9_2_3.title: Attending to others’ posts in asynchronous discussions: Learners’ online “listening” and its relationship to speaking
ijCSCL_9_2_3.authors: Alyssa Friend Wise & Simone Nicole Hausknecht & Yuting Zhao
ijCSCL_9_2_3.summary_haiku: Students' depth of listening—specifically rereading peers' posts—positively predicts responsiveness and argumentation quality in online discussions, while breadth alone does not. Using clickstream data from 31 undergraduates across six asynchronous discussions, multi-level regressions revealed that revisiting others' posts predicted more responsive comments, and reading (versus scanning) posts predicted richer argumentation. These listening-speaking relationships manifested differently across learner types over time.

ijCSCL_1_4_3.title: Electronic [re]constitution of groups: Group dynamics from face-to-face to an online setting
ijCSCL_1_4_3.authors: Lynn Clouder & Jayne Dalley & Julian Hargreaves & Sally Parkes & Julie Sellars & Jane Toms
ijCSCL_1_4_3.summary_haiku: This three-year case study examined how group dynamics change when physiotherapy students transition from face-to-face to online collaboration during clinical placements. Using action research with six seminar groups, researchers analyzed discussion forums, focus groups, and evaluations. Findings reveal that group dynamics remain relatively stable across contexts once established face-to-face, though individual participation may shift online. Social presence proves essential for positive dynamics, yet groups must transcend sociability to develop cognitive presence and deeper learning. Effective facilitation significantly influences outcomes, particularly when managing emotionally charged discussions or low-engagement groups.

ijCSCL_3_1_2.title: What does it mean? Students’ procedural and conceptual problem solving in a CSCL environment designed within the field of science education
ijCSCL_3_1_2.summary_haiku: This study examined procedural versus conceptual problem-solving in a CSCL environment where secondary students built a 3D insulin protein model using a codon table. Through interaction analysis of video-recorded collaborative sessions, researchers found that procedural problem-solving dominated student interactions, while conceptual knowledge construction occurred only when necessary for task completion. The authors conclude that institutional pressures to complete curriculum-based problems, combined with how the knowledge domain and tools were designed, prioritized procedural efficiency over deeper scientific understanding.

ijCSCL_1_2_5.title: Supporting synchronous collaborative learning: A generic, multi-dimensional model
ijCSCL_1_2_5.summary_haiku: Lonchamp proposes Omega+, a multi-dimensional model-based generic synchronous collaborative learning environment addressing limited applicability of existing CSCL systems. The system uses separate explicit models for collaborative situations, interactions, processes, and performance monitoring, enabling flexible combinations of scaffolding techniques. Evaluation occurs through functional equivalence demonstrations and a dedicated web platform supporting real-world usage analysis and teacher customization.

ijCSCL_3_3_0.title: Explorations of participation in discourse
ijCSCL_3_3_0.summary_haiku: This editorial examines how participation in discourse defines collaborative learning in CSCL research. It reviews studies analyzing student communication traces and discourse participation, highlighting challenges in automated analysis due to contextual dependencies. The articles featured demonstrate how technology design, scripting, and computational tools can support students' meaningful participation in disciplinary discourses across diverse learning contexts.

ijCSCL_8_4_0.title: Reigniting CSCL flash themes
ijCSCL_8_4_0.authors: Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse
ijCSCL_8_4_0.summary_haiku: This editorial introduces four emerging research themes in computer-supported collaborative learning: eye-tracking for joint attention, argumentation in gaming contexts, scripting with awareness prompts for collaborative drawing, and learning analytics with tabletop interfaces. The authors critically examine these studies, emphasizing that CSCL research must remain fundamentally concerned with human meaning-making practices mediated through designed artifacts, regardless of methodological sophistication.

ijCSCL_8_4_4.title: Capturing and analyzing verbal and physical collaborative learning interactions at an enriched interactive tabletop
ijCSCL_8_4_4.authors: Roberto Martinez-Maldonado & Yannis Dimitriadis & Alejandra Martinez-Monés & Judy Kay & Kalina Yacef
ijCSCL_8_4_4.summary_haiku: This study developed an approach to automatically capture and analyze verbal and physical interactions at an enriched interactive tabletop to distinguish collaborative from less collaborative student groups. Using sequence pattern mining on data from 60 students in concept-mapping triads, the researchers identified interaction patterns—including speech timing, turn-taking, and peer engagement—that differentiated high from low collaboration groups, demonstrating the potential of multimodal data analysis for supporting collaborative learning awareness.

ijCSCL_2_1_3.title: A rating scheme for assessing the quality of computer-supported collaboration processes
ijCSCL_2_1_3.authors: Anne Meier & Hans Spada & Nikol Rummel
ijCSCL_2_1_3.summary_haiku: Researchers developed a nine-dimension rating scheme for assessing computer-supported collaboration quality by combining qualitative analysis of student dialogue with theoretical frameworks. Applied to 40 dyads solving interdisciplinary patient cases via videoconferencing, the scheme demonstrated satisfactory inter-rater reliability and successfully detected instructional effects on collaboration processes, offering an efficient alternative to time-consuming transcription-based coding methods.

ijCSCL_3_3_4.title: The effect of a script and a structured interface in grounding discussions
ijCSCL_3_3_4.summary_haiku: This study examined how collaboration scripts and structured interfaces support grounding discussions among international students working remotely. Using a three-condition experiment (unscripted, script-only, script+interface), 42 students performed two grounding discussions structured into input, discussion, and consensus phases. Results showed scripts increased knowledge input quantity and discussion of differences, while structured interfaces further enhanced input length and adherence to prescribed activity sequences. However, no significant effects emerged for summary quality or learning outcomes.

ijCSCL_1_2_1.title: Approaching institutional contexts: Systemic versus dialogic research in CSCL
ijCSCL_1_2_1.summary_haiku: # Summary This article distinguishes between systemic and dialogic research approaches in CSCL to address how institutional contexts shape tool meanings and functions. Systemic approaches identify variable correlations affecting collaboration and outcomes, while dialogic approaches examine how meanings emerge through social interaction. The authors argue that dialogic analysis of sequential activities reveals why CSCL applications often fail in ordinary classrooms, demonstrating that understanding institutional practice transformation requires attention to how participants actively constitute contexts through their actions.

ijCSCL_9_4_1.title: Toward collaboration sensing
ijCSCL_9_4_1.summary_haiku: Researchers applied network analysis to dual eye-tracking data from collaborative learning dyads, representing fixations as nodes and saccades as edges. Network metrics correlated with collaboration quality dimensions, and machine learning algorithms predicted collaboration quality with 85-100% accuracy, suggesting eye-tracking networks can serve as "collaboration-sensing" tools for assessing and potentially improving student teamwork.

ijCSCL_8_2_2.title: Facilitating learning in multidisciplinary groups with transactive CSCL scripts
ijCSCL_8_2_2.authors: Omid Noroozi & Stephanie D. Teasley & Harm J. A. Biemans & Armin Weinberger & Martin Mulder
ijCSCL_8_2_2.summary_haiku: # Summary This laboratory experiment with 120 university students examined how transactive memory and discussion scripts in computer-supported collaborative learning environments facilitate knowledge sharing in multidisciplinary groups. Students from different disciplinary backgrounds solved an authentic problem requiring complementary expertise. Results showed that each script individually improved transactive knowledge sharing, knowledge transfer, and solution quality, but combining both scripts produced negative interaction effects, likely due to over-scripting constraints within the 80-minute collaboration period.

ijCSCL_8_2_3.title: Co-located single display collaborative learning for early childhood education
ijCSCL_8_2_3.authors: Florencia Gómez & Miguel Nussbaum & Juan F. Weitz & Ximena Lopez & Javiera Mena & Alex Torres
ijCSCL_8_2_3.summary_haiku: Small-group co-located single-display collaborative learning significantly improves oral language, logical-mathematical, and social skills in kindergarten children. Using a quasi-experimental design with 268 experimental and 172 control participants, researchers implemented computer-supported collaborative activities twice weekly for four months. Results showed the experimental group achieved substantially greater gains in logical-mathematical skills (21.78% vs. 6.09%) and social skills (10.09% vs. -8.19%), with teacher mediation proving essential for effective collaboration.

ijCSCL_1_2_0.title: Building knowledge in the classroom, building knowledge in the CSCL community
ijCSCL_1_2_0.summary_haiku: This editorial introduces the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning's second issue, presenting six articles addressing knowledge building in classrooms through collaborative learning with digital tools. The collection spans international research examining institutional context, design principles, narrative analysis, activity structures, and synchronous communication frameworks, demonstrating how pedagogy, technology, content, and theory must develop together in CSCL research.

ijCSCL_9_4_0.title: Analyzing roles of individuals in small-group collaboration processes
ijCSCL_9_4_0.authors: Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen
ijCSCL_9_4_0.summary_haiku: This editorial examines how computer-supported collaborative learning research analyzes individual roles within small groups. Four empirical studies employ diverse methodologies—eye-tracking analysis, interaction coding, social network analysis, and discourse analysis—to investigate joint attention, leadership, social roles, and uncertainty expressions. The papers collectively demonstrate that collaborative learning processes operate at multiple analytical levels, with group-level phenomena like shared intentionality and collective agency irreducible to individual cognition alone.

ijCSCL_3_3_5.title: Supporting students’ participation in authentic proof activities in computer supported collaborative learning (CSCL) environments Diler Öner
ijCSCL_3_3_5.summary_haiku: This paper proposes integrating dynamic geometry software with knowledge-building pedagogy in CSCL environments to support high school students' mathematical proof activities. The author argues that proof instruction should incorporate both empirical exploration and deductive reasoning, reflecting authentic mathematical practice. The study recommends software modifications, particularly adding shared dynamic geometry components and problematizing mechanisms, to help students distinguish between empirical conviction and formal proof while engaging in collaborative knowledge construction.

ijCSCL_2_1_2.title: Patterns as a paradigm for theory in community-based learning
ijCSCL_2_1_2.summary_haiku: Carroll and Farooq propose design patterns as a theoretical framework for understanding community-based IT learning. Through 12 years of participatory action research with volunteer organizations, they present two patterns: "Informal Developmental Learning" addresses lack of IT control through reflection, analysis, and enactment; "Scaffolded Documentation" manages knowledge loss from volunteer turnover via technology assessment, contingency planning, and lightweight documentation. Patterns serve as middle-level abstractions capturing recurring problems and solutions intelligible to practitioners themselves.

ijCSCL_2_1_0.title: Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2
ijCSCL_2_1_0.summary_haiku: This editorial marks ijCSCL's second volume, celebrating the journal's establishment as a vital communication venue for the CSCL community. Nearly one hundred papers were submitted globally, reviewed by two hundred researchers, demonstrating the field's maturation. The journal serves dual purposes: formal publication and constructive peer feedback, advancing collaborative learning research through rigorous editorial processes and community engagement.

ijCSCL_9_4_2.title: Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children’s collaborative learning groups
ijCSCL_9_4_2.authors: Emma M. Mercier & Steven E. Higgins & Laura da Costa
ijCSCL_9_4_2.summary_haiku: This study examines emergent leadership in children's collaborative learning groups through two investigations. Using a coding scheme adapted from prior research, the authors analyzed 32 students in Study One and 96 students in Study Two, identifying leadership moves as either intellectual (idea development, topic control) or organizational (turn management, planning). Results reveal leadership is distributed among group members, with approximately half of groups showing distinct intellectual and organizational leaders held by different students. Leadership patterns vary significantly across content areas and task types, suggesting leadership is context-dependent rather than stable.

ijCSCL_1_2_2.title: Collaborative knowledge building using the Design Principles Database
ijCSCL_1_2_2.summary_haiku: The Design Principles Database (DPD) supports collaborative knowledge building among educational technology researchers through a structured system of interconnected design features and principles at multiple abstraction levels. Using design-based research methodology across three iterations of a peer-evaluation activity, the study demonstrates how researchers extract principles from literature, test them in practice, and contribute refined knowledge back to the community database, exemplifying second-order collaborative learning environments.

ijCSCL_3_1_5.title: Group awareness and self-presentation in computer-supported information exchange
ijCSCL_3_1_5.summary_haiku: This experimental study examined how group awareness tools and protective self-presentation (PSP) influence knowledge-sharing behavior in computer-supported information exchange. Using a laboratory task simulating a social dilemma, 119 participants worked in three conditions: control, group-feedback, and individual-feedback. Results showed that individual feedback identifying each participant's contributions significantly increased cooperation rates, particularly among high-PSP individuals. An interaction effect emerged: high protective self-presenters were most cooperative when identifiable but least cooperative anonymously, suggesting self-presentation concerns drive knowledge-sharing behavior in collaborative digital environments.

ijCSCL_9_2_4.title: Preventing undesirable effects of mutual trust and the development of skepticism in virtual groups by applying the knowledge and information awareness approach
ijCSCL_9_2_4.authors: Tanja Engelmann & Richard Kolodziej & Friedrich W. Hesse
ijCSCL_9_2_4.summary_haiku: This experimental study examined whether a knowledge and information awareness (KIA) approach—providing digital concept maps of collaborators' knowledge—mitigates negative effects of mutual trust in virtual groups. Comparing 40 triads (20 with KIA, 20 without), researchers found that high initial trust reduced effectiveness in control groups but not experimental groups, while both conditions showed equal efficiency gains. Additionally, poor collaboration quality increased skepticism in control groups but not experimental groups, suggesting KIA facilitates mutual control independent of trust levels.

ijCSCL_1_4_4.title: Consistent practices in artifact-mediated collaboration
ijCSCL_1_4_4.summary_haiku: This study examined how dyads collaboratively solve problems using flexible paper-based media while restricted to written communication. Through video analysis of six pairs discussing wicked problems, researchers identified invariant communicative practices across different materials and participants. Despite varied interaction styles and artifacts, consistent patterns emerged in managing attention, awareness, and ownership of contributions. Findings challenge conventional CSCL design assumptions and suggest that effective collaborative technologies should support flexible semiotic resources rather than rigid representational structures.

ijCSCL_8_2_1.title: Participation and common knowledge in a case study of student blogging
ijCSCL_8_2_1.summary_haiku: This case study examines how student blogging facilitates common knowledge emergence in a loosely coordinated learning environment. Through qualitative and quantitative analysis of 25 undergraduates' semester-long blogging activity in an Internet & Society course, researchers found that common knowledge develops through distributed participation across multiple conversations and topics. Longer conversations served as focal points attracting wider readership and participation, while persistent content enabled students to mine the blogosphere when preparing papers, with approximately 50% of paper topics foreshadowed by blogging activity.

ijCSCL_8_2_0.title: Transactive discourse in CSCL
ijCSCL_8_2_0.summary_haiku: This editorial examines transactivity in computer-supported collaborative learning, analyzing how students build on each other's reasoning through shared digital media. Stahl distinguishes between individual-level analysis focusing on mental states and group-level analysis examining discourse meaning. Four empirical studies explore transactivity across contexts—student blogging, scripted dyadic interactions, kindergarten collaborative computer use, and automated speech analysis—demonstrating diverse methodological approaches to measuring and supporting collaborative knowledge building.

ijCSCL_3_1_4.title: The need for considering multilevel analysis in CSCL research—An appeal for the use of more advanced statistical methods
ijCSCL_3_1_4.summary_haiku: CSCL research involves hierarchically nested data—individuals within groups—yet standard statistical methods violate independence assumptions, causing alpha-error inflation. Multilevel modeling (MLM) addresses this by simultaneously analyzing individual and group levels, testing cross-level interactions between within-group predictors and between-group variables. However, MLM requires large sample sizes typically unavailable in CSCL studies, necessitating alternative approaches and careful reporting of intraclass correlations.

ijCSCL_9_4_3.title: “Newbies” and “Celebrities”: Detecting social roles in an online network of teachers via participation patterns
ijCSCL_9_4_3.summary_haiku: This study used cluster analysis combining structural and behavioral data to identify social roles in an unstructured online teacher blog network. Analyzing 99 teachers' participation patterns across six months, researchers detected five distinct roles: "Newbies," "Inbound Participants," "Full Participants," "Celebrities," and "Peripheral Members." Results revealed that participation patterns and network position significantly influence both current role and trajectory of role change, with expertise and engagement type affecting status transitions independent of tenure.

ijCSCL_1_2_3.title: Co-reﬂection in online learning: Collaborative critical thinking as narrative
ijCSCL_1_2_3.summary_haiku: This study examined two graduate students' learning in an online action research course using narrative analysis. The research identifies co-reflection—a collaborative critical thinking process combining cognitive and affective interactions with relationship building—as central to knowledge co-construction. Two co-reflection types emerged: tacit (indirect, subtle) and active (explicit, discursive). Simple, flexible software tools effectively supported inquiry learning by accommodating diverse communication and learning styles.

ijCSCL_2_1_1.title: Community-based learning: The core competency of residential, research-based universities
ijCSCL_2_1_1.authors: Gerhard Fischer & Markus Rohde & Volker Wulf
ijCSCL_2_1_1.summary_haiku: Residential research universities can maintain competitive advantage against online education by adopting community-based learning grounded in socio-cultural theory. The authors present case studies from University of Colorado and University of Siegen demonstrating how integrating students into communities of practice through apprenticeships, peer collaboration, and regional industry partnerships creates meaningful learning experiences that transcend traditional instructionist models, requiring significant cultural change and faculty risk-taking.

ijCSCL_3_3_6.title: Book review: Exploring thinking as communicating in CSCL
ijCSCL_3_3_6.summary_haiku: Sfard's theory conceptualizes mathematical objects as products of discursive processes rather than mental acquisitions, arguing that deep understanding emerges through participation in social routines of mathematical discourse. The review examines how students collaboratively construct mathematical meaning through communication, proposing that extending this participationist framework to computer-mediated group interaction could advance CSCL research while requiring integration with broader social and cultural dimensions.

ijCSCL_9_1_0.title: Analyzing the multidimensional construction of knowledge in diverse contexts
ijCSCL_9_1_0.authors: Gerry Stahl & Ulrike Cress & Nancy Law & Sten Ludvigsen
ijCSCL_9_1_0.summary_haiku: This editorial examines how knowledge is constructed across multiple levels—individual, small-group, and community—in diverse learning contexts. Through Activity Theory, knowledge-building games, Knowledge Forum analysis, and Wikipedia research, the authors demonstrate that collaborative knowledge construction relies on interactional resources and artifacts that bridge different analytical scales, from classroom discourse to global online communities.

ijCSCL_8_1_5.title: Enhancing student knowledge acquisition from online learning conversations
ijCSCL_8_1_5.authors: Evren Eryilmaz & Jakko van der Pol & Terry Ryan & Philip Martin Clark & Justin Mary
ijCSCL_8_1_5.summary_haiku: This experimental study compared linked and parallel artifact-centered discussion systems with 106 pharmacy students. Annotation functionality in the linked system decreased coordination activities while increasing assertion and conflict knowledge construction activities. Mediation analysis revealed that assertion, conflict, and clarification activities significantly predicted individual learning gains, with the treatment group achieving greater post-test improvements than controls.

ijCSCL_9_3_2.title: How to bring a technical artifact into use: A micro-developmental perspective
ijCSCL_9_3_2.authors: Maarten Overdijk & Wouter van Diggelen & Jerry Andriessen & Paul A. Kirschner
ijCSCL_9_3_2.summary_haiku: # Summary This micro-developmental case study examines how a student pair appropriated a digital shared workspace for project planning. Using qualitative analysis of classroom observations, interviews, and interaction protocols, the research reveals that artifact appropriation involves tension between existing classroom practices and new tool affordances. Resistance from the artifact—when it contradicted established planning conventions—triggered reflection and procedural adaptation, while absence of resistance enabled unreflective departures from regular practice. The findings demonstrate that technology use emerges through complex negotiations between learner intentions and designer intentions embedded in artifacts.

ijCSCL_2_4_2.title: Future technology workshop: A collaborative method for the design of new learning technologies and activities
ijCSCL_2_4_2.summary_haiku: The Future Technology Workshop (FTW) is a collaborative design method enabling participants with domain knowledge to envision and prototype interactions between current/future technologies and activities. Through seven structured sessions combining brainstorming, low-tech prototyping, role-play, and scenario analysis, participants progress from imagining far-future possibilities to grounding ideas in present constraints, ultimately generating implementable technology requirements. Successfully applied with children and adults across multiple projects, FTW provides cost-effective, pragmatic outcomes directly informing human-centered systems design.

ijCSCL_1_3_4.title: Studying participation networks in collaboration using mixed methods
ijCSCL_1_3_4.authors: AlejandraMartínez & Yannis Dimitriadis & Eduardo Gómez-Sánchez & Bartolomé Rubia-Avi & Iván Jorrín-Abellán & Jose A. Marcos
ijCSCL_1_3_4.summary_haiku: This study validates a mixed-evaluation method combining social network analysis with qualitative and quantitative approaches to assess participatory learning in CSCL contexts. Applied across three diverse scenarios—blended learning, distance learning, and synchronous collaboration—the method demonstrates flexibility and appropriateness for measuring interaction structures. Results confirm that integrating multiple data sources and analysis techniques provides efficient, reliable evaluation while remaining accessible to practitioners, though resource demands remain substantial.

ijCSCL_2_2_4.title: Specifying computer-supported collaboration scripts
ijCSCL_2_2_4.authors: Lars Kobbe & Armin Weinberger & Pierre Dillenbourg & Andreas Harrer & Raija Hämäläinen & Päivi Häkkinen & Frank Fischer
ijCSCL_2_2_4.summary_haiku: This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for specifying computer-supported collaboration scripts by consolidating prior approaches. Through conceptual analysis, the authors identify five core components (participants, activities, roles, resources, groups) and three mechanisms (task distribution, group formation, sequencing) that enable platform-independent script description. The framework facilitates systematic research, practical design, and computational formalization of collaborative learning scripts across diverse educational contexts.

ijCSCL_1_1_6.title: A dialogic understanding of the relationship between CSCL and teaching thinking skills
ijCSCL_1_1_6.summary_haiku: # Summary Wegerif argues that dialogue itself constitutes the primary thinking skill underlying creativity and learning-to-learn. Through literature review and case studies using Raven's reasoning tests, he demonstrates that teaching dialogue as an end in itself—rather than as a tool for knowledge construction—promotes general thinking skills. He proposes a dialogic interpretative framework for CSCL that emphasizes opening, deepening, and broadening reflective spaces through technology-supported dialogue.

ijCSCL_3_2_1.title: A systemic and cognitive view on collaborative knowledge building with wikis
ijCSCL_3_2_1.summary_haiku: This article presents a theoretical framework integrating Luhmann's systems theory with Piaget's equilibration theory to explain collaborative knowledge building in wikis. The model distinguishes between social and cognitive systems, analyzing how externalization and internalization processes enable learning through assimilation and accommodation. Empirical Wikipedia examples demonstrate that medium-level incongruities between individual knowledge and wiki content motivate equilibration activities, driving both individual learning and collaborative knowledge building through co-evolution of systems.

ijCSCL_3_2_0.title: The strength of the lone wolf
ijCSCL_3_2_0.summary_haiku: This editorial examines the dialectical relationship between individual and group in computer-supported collaborative learning. Through conceptual analysis of five research papers addressing wikis, group feedback, annotations, argumentation scripts, and macro-scripts, the author argues that CSCL technology must mediate the intersubjective-to-individual learning process. The papers demonstrate how specific tools shape both individual cognition and collaborative group practices.

ijCSCL_2_2_5.title: Scripting by assigning roles: Does it improve knowledge construction in asynchronous discussion groups?
ijCSCL_2_2_5.authors: Tammy Schellens & Hilde Van Keer & Bram De Wever & Martin Valcke
ijCSCL_2_2_5.summary_haiku: This design-based research compared two cohorts of university students (N=223 and N=286) across consecutive academic years to examine whether assigning rotating roles in asynchronous discussion groups enhances knowledge construction. Using multilevel analysis of coded discussion transcripts and exam scores, results showed that role assignment significantly improved students' knowledge construction levels and final exam performance, with an effect size of 0.5 standard deviations. However, differential effects emerged by role type, with summarizers benefiting most.

ijCSCL_2_4_3.title: Facilitating argumentative knowledge construction with computer-supported collaboration scripts
ijCSCL_2_4_3.authors: Karsten Stegmann & Armin Weinberger & Frank Fischer
ijCSCL_2_4_3.summary_haiku: Computer-supported collaboration scripts significantly improve argumentative knowledge construction in online discussions. A 2×2 factorial study with 120 educational science students examined scripts supporting single argument construction and argumentation sequences. Results showed scripts substantially enhanced formal argument quality and argumentation sequence quality. Scripts also facilitated knowledge on argumentation but not domain-specific knowledge, suggesting learners focused effort on argumentation skills rather than content mastery.

ijCSCL_9_3_3.title: An examination of CSCL methodological practices and the influence of theoretical frameworks 2005–2009
ijCSCL_9_3_3.authors: Heisawn Jeong & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Yawen Yu
ijCSCL_9_3_3.summary_haiku: This content analysis examined methodological practices in 400 empirical CSCL studies published 2005–2009 across seven leading journals. Researchers coded studies across research designs, settings, data sources, and analysis methods, then examined relationships with theoretical frameworks. Findings revealed descriptive designs dominated (54%), classroom settings predominated (74%), and quantitative analysis was most common (86%), though qualitative and mixed methods were frequent. Cluster analysis identified four distinctive method-theory combinations, demonstrating that theoretical frameworks significantly influenced methodological choices across all dimensions.

ijCSCL_8_1_4.title: Recalibrating reference within a dual-space interaction environment
ijCSCL_8_1_4.summary_haiku: # Summary Middle school students collaborating in the Virtual Math Teams system develop shared understanding of mathematical problems through sequential recalibration of referential practices. Using ethnomethodological analysis of chat and whiteboard interactions, the study demonstrates how students progressively specify indexical properties of underspecified problems and solutions. Rather than treating representations as static objects, the research reveals how problem-solving emerges from the situated, interactive work of producing and refining references to mathematical concepts across dual-space modalities.

ijCSCL_9_1_1.title: The dialectical potential of Cultural Historical Activity Theory for researching sustainable CSCL practices
ijCSCL_9_1_1.summary_haiku: Cultural Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) offers a relational, dialectical framework for understanding sustainable computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) in authentic educational settings. This study proposes an integrated CHAT methodology that moves beyond descriptive triangle models to analyze contradictions and tensions across multiple activity levels. Through a five-stage analytical process applied to undergraduate online collaboration, the research demonstrates how CHAT's dialectical method reveals complex interrelations between discourse, actions, and community, explaining why collaborative practices succeed or fail to become institutionalized.

ijCSCL_9_1_3.title: Multi-player epistemic games: Guiding the enactment of classroom knowledge-building communities
ijCSCL_9_1_3.summary_haiku: Researchers extended epistemic games—strategic knowledge-building practices—to "multi-player" versions where students collectively advance ideas through distributed contributions in Knowledge Forum. Using design-based research in Singapore primary science classrooms, they developed scaffolding tools (Think Cards and hypothetical game-configurations) to help students learn the Progressive-Improvement Game. Analyses showed students improved significantly in generating valid knowledge-building moves, supporting classroom enactment of knowledge-building communities.

ijCSCL_8_3_4.title: Inducing socio-cognitive conflict in Finnish and German groups of online learners by CSCL script
ijCSCL_8_3_4.authors: Armin Weinberger & Miika Marttunen & Leena Laurinen & Karsten Stegmann
ijCSCL_8_3_4.summary_haiku: This cross-cultural study examined how a peer-critique collaboration script affects socio-cognitive conflict in online learning. Using a 2×2 design with 132 Finnish and German university students, researchers analyzed discussion patterns and knowledge acquisition. Results revealed German groups engaged in more conflict-oriented consensus building than Finnish groups, who preferred integration-oriented approaches. The script strengthened conflict-oriented discourse in German groups but proved incompatible with Finnish collaborative norms, suggesting CSCL environments require culturally sensitive design.

ijCSCL_3_4_4.title: Alternative goal structures for computer game-based learning
ijCSCL_3_4_4.summary_haiku: This field study examined how cooperative, competitive, and individualistic goal structures in classroom computer math games affect fifth-graders' math performance and attitudes. Using a pretest-posttest design with 160 students across four conditions, results showed all gaming groups outperformed controls on math tests, but cooperative goal structures proved most effective for promoting positive math attitudes. Socioeconomic status significantly moderated outcomes, with disadvantaged students benefiting most from cooperation.

ijCSCL_9_3_1.title: The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration Crina I. Damşa
ijCSCL_9_3_1.summary_haiku: # Summary This study examines productive interactions in small-group collaborative learning through a 20-week undergraduate research project. Using qualitative analysis and descriptive statistics, the researcher analyzed five student groups' interactions and emerging knowledge objects (research reports). Findings reveal that productive interactions manifest in two primary patterns: discourse-based interactions fostering shared understanding, and object-oriented interactions involving iterative co-construction. Groups demonstrating shared epistemic agency—deliberate, joint engagement with knowledge materialization—produced higher-quality knowledge objects, suggesting that productive collaboration integrates discursive interaction with tangible object development over time.

ijCSCL_2_4_1.title: Using activity-oriented design methods to study collaborative knowledge-building in e-learning courses within higher education
ijCSCL_2_4_1.summary_haiku: Activity-Oriented Design Methods (AODM) operationalize Activity Theory to analyze collaborative knowledge-building in e-learning courses. Using qualitative case study methodology, researchers applied AODM's six-stage framework to examine course design teams and students in online higher education. Findings revealed that peer collaboration, facilitated through small-group assignments and discussion guidelines, supported students' development of statistical knowledge through exploratory talk and iterative refinement of shared learning objects.

ijCSCL_2_2_7.title: How do argumentation diagrams compare when student pairs use them as a means for debate or as a tool for representing debate?
ijCSCL_2_2_7.authors: Kristine Lund & Gaëlle Molinari & Arnauld Séjourné & Michael Baker
ijCSCL_2_2_7.summary_haiku: This study compared two instructional approaches for using argumentation diagrams during online debates among 36 secondary students. Using the ADAM analysis method, researchers examined individual diagrams created before and after debate, plus collaborative diagrams produced during debate. Results revealed that students instructed to represent their chat debate in diagrams added more non-argumentative relations (examples, causes, consequences), while those using diagrams simultaneously during debate expressed more opinions about arguments. These findings suggest different cognitive mechanisms emerge depending on whether diagrams mediate debate or represent completed debate.

ijCSCL_1_1_5.title: R-U-Typing-2-Me? Evolving a chat tool to increase understanding in learning activities
ijCSCL_1_1_5.authors: Hugo Fuks & Mariano Pimentel & Carlos Jose´ Pereira de Lucena
ijCSCL_1_1_5.summary_haiku: This research investigates "Chat Confusion"—difficulties following conversations when multiple participants communicate simultaneously in chat tools used for educational debates. Through iterative design-based development, researchers identified six key problems: co-text loss, dynamics interruption, message overload, lack-of-visibility-of-turn-in-progress, reading difficulties, and decontextualization. Successive Mediated Chat versions implemented targeted solutions including message threading, structured conversation techniques, publication queues, interface improvements, and session history. Case studies demonstrated that combining structured dynamics with interface enhancements effectively reduced confusion and improved understanding in online learning activities.

ijCSCL_3_2_2.title: Supporting controversial CSCL discussions with augmented group awareness tools
ijCSCL_3_2_2.summary_haiku: Augmented group awareness tools that aggregate and visualize learner ratings of discussion contributions can strengthen minority influence in collaborative learning. An experimental study with groups discussing controversial physics topics found that groups using rating-based awareness tools made significantly better decisions and showed higher individual learning than unsupported groups, particularly by shifting majority members toward scientifically correct minority viewpoints through enhanced informational influence.

ijCSCL_3_2_3.title: Annotations and the collaborative digital library: Effects of an aligned annotation interface on student argumentation and reading strategies
ijCSCL_3_2_3.summary_haiku: Aligned annotation interfaces—where reader comments appear in text margins—significantly enhance student critical thinking and argumentation. Two complementary studies found that annotations, particularly pairs presenting conflicting viewpoints, prompted students to move beyond passive comprehension toward active evaluation and perspective-taking. Students receiving annotated materials demonstrated reduced reliance on summary strategies and greater engagement with competing positions, suggesting annotations provide valuable scaffolding for developing critical reading and writing practices.

ijCSCL_1_1_4.title: Situating CoWeb: a scholarship of application
ijCSCL_1_1_4.summary_haiku: Researchers developed CoWeb, a wiki-based platform for collaborative learning, and deployed it across diverse academic contexts at Georgia Tech. Through design-based research, they found that collaborative learning success depends critically on cultural compatibility: CoWeb succeeded in architecture and composition where collaboration aligned with disciplinary values, but failed in STEM courses due to competitive cultures. By redesigning an introductory computing course around collaborative principles, they overcame these barriers, demonstrating that culture can be intentionally shaped to support technology adoption.

ijCSCL_2_2_6.title: Using graphical tools in a phased activity for enhancing dialogical skills: An example with Digalo
ijCSCL_2_2_6.authors: Nathalie Muller Mirza & Valérie Tartas & Anne-Nelly Perret-Clermont & Jean-François de Pietro
ijCSCL_2_2_6.summary_haiku: This study examined how university students developed argumentative and historical knowledge through a phased learning activity using Digalo, graphical argument-mapping software. Using descriptive analysis of two collective debates about the Valladolid Controversy, researchers found that students constructed complex understanding of the historical topic while developing sophisticated argument-counterargument-reply sequences. The software's visual representations and structured functionalities supported both topic meaning-making and argumentative processes, enabling students to elaborate justifications and integrate opposing perspectives into their reasoning.

ijCSCL_2_4_0.title: CSCL and its flash themes
ijCSCL_2_4_0.summary_haiku: Stahl examines how "flash themes"—coordinated collections of papers on emerging research topics—develop within the CSCL community through collaborative, iterative processes involving workshops, peer review, and journal publication. Using a dialectical metaphor of logs and fire, he argues that scientific ideas emerge not from individual minds but through situated, institutionally-mediated interactions among researchers, editors, and the broader academic community.

ijCSCL_9_3_0.title: CSCL artifacts
ijCSCL_9_3_0.authors: Gerry Stahl & Sten Ludvigsen & Nancy Law & Ulrike Cress
ijCSCL_9_3_0.summary_haiku: Artifacts are central to computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL), serving multiple roles including communication media, knowledge representation structures, and collaborative products. This editorial examines how artifacts mediate group meaning-making processes and presents four papers analyzing artifact roles in CSCL settings and trends in CSCL research publications, advancing understanding of the post-cognitive CSCL paradigm emphasizing group-level processes over individual learning outcomes.

ijCSCL_3_4_5.title: Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols
ijCSCL_3_4_5.summary_haiku: Researchers developed an automatic coding system to identify dialogue acts (communicative functions) in online collaboration protocols using discourse markers. Testing on 1,000 messages showed 79% agreement with manual coding (Cohen's kappa=0.75). Validity analyses confirmed the system reliably distinguished gender differences in communication patterns and detected experimental intervention effects, supporting its utility for analyzing collaborative learning processes.

ijCSCL_8_3_5.title: Dialogical positions as a method of understanding identity trajectories in a collaborative blended university course
ijCSCL_8_3_5.authors: M. Beatrice Ligorio & Fedela Feldia Loperfido & Nadia Sansone
ijCSCL_8_3_5.summary_haiku: # Summary This study proposes a three-step qualitative-quantitative method for tracking identity trajectories in collaborative learning using Bakhtinian concepts of polyphony and chronotopes as dialogical indicators. Applied to online notes from two university students in a blended course, the method reveals unique, context-sensitive identity development patterns, demonstrating how students' positioning shifts across course modules in response to activities and personal circumstances.

ijCSCL_8_3_1.title: Vocational education approach: New TEL settings—new prospects for teachers’ instructional activities?
ijCSCL_8_3_1.summary_haiku: This design-based research study examined vocational teachers' instructional activities in a 3D game environment using content analysis of 8,188 utterances from four teacher-student groups. Findings revealed teachers employed two distinct approaches: "knowledge-providing" and "joint problem-solving," with different student responses. Teachers asked more contextual questions and engaged in shared problem-solving than students, while students provided more knowledge. The study demonstrates teachers spontaneously develop innovative instructional strategies in technology-enhanced vocational learning settings, shifting from classroom management toward empowering collaborative knowledge construction.

ijCSCL_3_4_1.title: Leveraging online communities in fostering adaptive schools
ijCSCL_3_4_1.authors: David Hung & Kenneth Y. T. Lim & Der-Thanq Victor Chen & Thiam Seng Koh
ijCSCL_3_4_1.summary_haiku: Online communities function as "para-communities" that should remain distinct from formal schools rather than being integrated into them. Through conceptual analysis, the authors argue that schools and online communities serve fundamentally different goals: schools emphasize intentional learning and efficiency, while online communities prioritize intrinsic motivation and innovation. They propose that adaptive schools leverage external para-communities through internal Communities of Interest, enabling complementary relationships that cultivate social capital and innovation without compromising organizational efficiency.

ijCSCL_9_3_4.title: Contemporary intellectual structure of CSCL research (2006–2013): a co-citation network analysis with an education focus
ijCSCL_9_3_4.authors: Kai-Yu Tang & Chin-Chung Tsai & Tzu-Chiang Lin
ijCSCL_9_3_4.summary_haiku: This study employed document co-citation analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and social network analysis to map the intellectual structure of CSCL research (2006–2013). Analyzing 403 source papers and 5,351 citing articles, researchers identified six research subfields: representation and discourse patterns, factors influencing CSCL, intervention and comparison, critical reasoning, social construction processes, and design and modeling. Results revealed seminal works and core publications, with representation and discourse emerging as the dominant research stream, demonstrating the field's maturity and interconnectedness.

ijCSCL_8_1_3.title: Student sensemaking with science diagrams in a computer-based setting
ijCSCL_8_1_3.authors: Anniken Furberg & Anders Kluge & Sten Ludvigsen
ijCSCL_8_1_3.summary_haiku: This study examined how upper secondary students collaboratively made sense of solar panel diagrams in a computer-based learning environment. Using interaction analysis of one student group's expert-group session, researchers found that science diagrams functioned as productive social and cognitive resources, enabling students to slow conceptual reasoning and negotiate scientific meanings. However, students faced significant challenges translating oral accounts into written explanations and coordinating multiple diagram representations. The analysis reveals that students' sensemaking involved not only conceptual understanding but also navigating institutional norms and practices embedded within schooling contexts.

ijCSCL_2_4_4.title: The role of floor control and of ontology in argumentative activities with discussion-based tools
ijCSCL_2_4_4.summary_haiku: This study examined how informal argumentative ontologies and floor control in synchronous e-discussions affect knowledge co-elaboration among 54 seventh-grade students using the Digalo tool.
