Using a 2×2 factorial design, researchers compared conditions with/without ontology and with/without floor control. Results showed that combining informal ontology with floor control produced significantly more relevant claims and arguments while reducing chat-style expressions and non-productive peer references, suggesting these design features facilitate collaborative knowledge construction.

ijCSCL_1_3_2.title: The affordance of anchored discussion for the collaborative processing of academic texts
ijCSCL_1_3_2.authors: J. van der Pol & W. Admiraal & P.R.J. Simons
ijCSCL_1_3_2.summary_haiku: Anchored discussion systems, which integrate texts directly into online forums with message anchoring capabilities, promote more text-focused and constructive collaboration than traditional forum discussion. Comparing these systems with standard discussion boards in a pedagogy course, the study found anchored discussion produced more meaning-oriented discourse, more efficient communication, and fewer social digressions, making it more suitable for collaborative academic text comprehension among undergraduate students.

ijCSCL_2_2_2.title: Supporting collaborative learning and problem-solving in a constraint-based CSCL environment for UML class diagrams
ijCSCL_2_2_2.authors: Nilufar Baghaei & Antonija Mitrovic & Warwick Irwin
ijCSCL_2_2_2.summary_haiku: COLLECT-UML is a constraint-based intelligent tutoring system that teaches UML class diagram design while supporting collaborative learning. Using meta-constraints to model collaboration alongside domain constraints, the system provides feedback on both problem-solving and teamwork. Evaluation studies with 48 students showed significant improvements in UML knowledge and collaboration skills, with experimental group participants acquiring greater declarative knowledge about effective collaboration and demonstrating more balanced, active participation.

ijCSCL_1_1_0.title: ijCSCL—a journal for research in CSCL
ijCSCL_1_1_0.summary_haiku: The International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (ijCSCL) was established to advance the maturing CSCL field by providing a peer-reviewed publication venue for an increasingly global research community. The journal aims to foster interdisciplinary collaboration, develop CSCL-specific theories and methodologies, and disseminate high-quality research through open-access online platforms alongside traditional publication formats.

ijCSCL_1_1_1.title: The CSCL community in its ﬁrst decade: development, continuity, connectivity
ijCSCL_1_1_1.summary_haiku: The CSCL community's first decade (1995–2005) demonstrates growth and increasing internationalization despite low individual continuity. Using quantitative analysis of conference proceedings, participant lists, and program committees combined with qualitative surveys, researchers found that while 79% of authors contributed to only one conference, international connectivity grew substantially through citations and co-authorships across countries, with conference location rotation and diverse program committee composition supporting this development.

ijCSCL_2_2_3.title: Dealing with multiple documents on the WWW: The role of metacognition in the formation of documents models
ijCSCL_2_2_3.summary_haiku: This study examined whether metacognitive prompting helps laypersons form documents models—integrated representations of content and sources—when researching medical information online. Using an experimental design with 79 participants assigned to groups receiving evaluation prompts, monitoring prompts, both, or neither, researchers found that monitoring prompts enhanced factual knowledge acquisition, while evaluation prompts improved source knowledge and source attribution in essays, supporting metacognition's importance in multiple-document comprehension.

ijCSCL_1_3_3.title: Code talk: Student discourse and participation with networked handhelds
ijCSCL_1_3_3.summary_haiku: Networked handheld computers in a middle school mathematics classroom expanded collaborative problem-solving participation beyond traditional discourse. Through interactional analysis of two student groups using the Code Breaker cryptography software, the study found that students demonstrating largest achievement gains gave more instructions and responded less frequently. Importantly, shared mathematical objects across devices enabled non-discursive participation forms, allowing lower-status students to contribute meaningfully despite limited verbal participation.

ijCSCL_2_4_5.title: Putting the pieces together: Online argumentation vee diagrams enhance thinking during discussions
ijCSCL_2_4_5.authors: E. Michael Nussbaum & Denise L. Winsor & Yvette M. Aqui & Anne M. Poliquin
ijCSCL_2_4_5.summary_haiku: Online argumentation vee diagrams (AVDs) significantly enhance students' ability to integrate opposing arguments in asynchronous discussions. Using a quasi-experimental design with 87 preservice teachers, students completing individual AVDs before discussions and collaborative group AVDs afterward demonstrated greater compromise-based reasoning and opinion change compared to controls. Scaffolding questions evaluating argument strength proved essential for effectiveness, suggesting structured support facilitates metacognitive reflection necessary for balanced argumentation.

ijCSCL_8_1_2.title: On the bridge to learn: Analysing the social organization of nautical instruction in a ship simulator
ijCSCL_8_1_2.summary_haiku: This qualitative study examines how nautical students collaboratively construct simulated learning contexts through role-play in a ship simulator. Using interaction analysis of video data, the researchers identify two competing activity contexts: students enacting professional crew roles and students participating in educational training. The analysis reveals that while role-play enables situated learning opportunities for professional tasks, maintaining credible simulations requires substantial interactional effort and can conflict with instructional objectives like meta-reflection and debriefing.

ijCSCL_3_4_0.title: CSCL practices
ijCSCL_3_4_0.summary_haiku: This editorial examines computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) practices across educational contexts. It synthesizes research on how collaborative learning emerges through technology-mediated interactions at individual, group, and community levels. Key findings address student self-efficacy in science, game-based math learning outcomes, and automated analysis methods for collaborative discourse, emphasizing that effective CSCL implementation requires attention to surrounding pedagogical and social practices.

ijCSCL_8_3_0.title: Collaborative Learning at CSCL 2013
ijCSCL_8_3_0.authors: Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse
ijCSCL_8_3_0.summary_haiku: The CSCL 2013 conference brought together international researchers to advance collaborative learning research and practice. A presidential symposium analyzed regional developments in North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia, revealing diverse research approaches unified by a common goal: improving collaborative learning implementation in education. The field faces opportunities through initiatives like PISA's planned assessment of collaborative problem-solving skills.

ijCSCL_8_3_2.title: Crossing boundaries in Facebook: Students’ framing of language learning activities as extended spaces
ijCSCL_8_3_2.authors: Annika Lantz-Andersson & Sylvi Vigmo & Rhonwen Bowen
ijCSCL_8_3_2.summary_haiku: This ethnographic case study examined how 60 students aged 13-16 from four countries framed English language learning activities in a Facebook group. Using frame analysis and sociocultural theory, researchers found that students initially adopted formal school-task framing but gradually negotiated boundary-crossing interactions creating extended learning spaces. However, maintaining these dynamic spaces proved difficult, requiring deliberate collaborative negotiation between educators and students to balance everyday social media practices with educational goals.

ijCSCL_3_4_2.title: The right tool for the wrong task? Match and mismatch between first and second stimulus in double stimulation
ijCSCL_3_4_2.summary_haiku: This study examines how Norwegian high school students learning English as a foreign language approach open-ended collaborative tasks using wiki technology. Using Vygotsky's double stimulation framework, researchers analyzed the relationship between task design (first stimulus) and available tools (second stimulus) in collaborative knowledge construction. Findings reveal that learners struggled to maintain awareness across individual, group, and whole-class levels. When the wiki application failed, students sustained collective working practices through alternative tools like PowerPoint and MSN chat, demonstrating that pedagogical and technological designs must be better aligned to support collaborative knowledge production.

ijCSCL_8_1_0.title: Analyzing group coordination when solving geometry problems with dynamic geometry software
ijCSCL_8_1_0.summary_haiku: This study proposes a methodological framework for analyzing group coordination in geometry problem-solving with dynamic geometry software. Using conversation analysis and reference field theory, the researcher examined a dyad's face-to-face interaction solving a construction problem. Findings reveal successful collaboration requires coordinating both mathematical/tool-enabled resources and collaborative resources, with participants shifting between theoretical and spatio-graphical reference fields while maintaining productive turn-taking and transactive dialogue.

ijCSCL_1_3_1.title: Technology affordances for intersubjective meaning making: A research agenda for CSCL Daniel D. Suthers
ijCSCL_1_3_1.authors: making: A research agenda for CSCL Daniel D. Suthers
ijCSCL_1_3_1.summary_haiku: Suthers proposes intersubjective meaning making—how groups jointly compose interpretations of dynamically evolving contexts—as CSCL's integrating research agenda. Through conceptual analysis, he argues that technology should be designed as fundamentally social to afford such meaning-making processes. He advocates hybrid methodologies combining experimental, descriptive, and design approaches, with "uptake" relations serving as a boundary object enabling dialogue across theoretical traditions.

ijCSCL_2_2_1.title: Contextual perspective in analysing collaborative knowledge construction of two small groups in web-based discussion
ijCSCL_2_2_1.summary_haiku: This study presents a methodology for analyzing collaborative knowledge construction in asynchronous web-based discussions by examining two student groups' thematic structure, communicative functions, and contextual resources. Comparing novice and experienced teacher-education students, findings reveal that different backgrounds influenced how groups created and interpreted context, negotiated meanings, and selected resources—novices relied on course material and peer discussion, while experienced students drew primarily on personal teaching experience.

ijCSCL_1_1_3.title: Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building
ijCSCL_1_1_3.authors: Eddy Y.C. Lee & Carol K.K. Chan & Jan van Aalst
ijCSCL_1_1_3.summary_haiku: This study examined how electronic portfolio assessments guided by knowledge-building principles support collaborative inquiry in computer forums. Using a quasi-experimental design with 119 ninth-grade students across three Knowledge Forum conditions, researchers found that students receiving portfolios with knowledge-building principles demonstrated deeper inquiry, more high-level questions, and superior conceptual understanding compared to peers using forums alone or portfolios without principles. Portfolio scores predicted essay performance beyond individual participation metrics, suggesting portfolios effectively capture distributed, progressive knowledge advancement.

ijCSCL_3_2_4.title: Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application
ijCSCL_3_2_4.summary_haiku: This case study examines how student groups appropriate a graphical shared workspace during computer-mediated argumentative discussion. Through micro-analysis of tool-mediated interactions, the researchers found that groups develop shared organizational principles through implicit negotiation of conventions. Four groups demonstrated distinct orientations—maintaining direct interaction, constructing personal reasoning, or submitting unrelated contributions—resulting in different principles for organizing contributions. The study reveals mutual shaping between students and tool, where early choices constrain later possibilities and strong graphical principles prove difficult to abandon.

ijCSCL_3_2_5.title: Operationalizing macro-scripts in CSCL technological settings
ijCSCL_3_2_5.summary_haiku: This article proposes SPAIRD, a conceptualization model for operationalizing CSCL macro-scripts—pedagogical activity structures that guide collaborative learning. The research identifies core design dimensions including script reification through technology, student presentation strategies, and uncertainties in script perception and enactment. SPAIRD disentangles structural models, implementation models, platform specifications, and student-oriented models while documenting design rationale. The analysis examines current technological approaches and advocates for flexible, model-based script engines supporting iterative design.

ijCSCL_1_1_2.title: A relational, indirect, meso-level approach to CSCL design in the next decade
ijCSCL_1_1_2.authors: Chris Jones & Lone Dirckinck<Holmfeld & Berner Lindstro¨m
ijCSCL_1_1_2.summary_haiku: This theoretical paper proposes a relational approach to CSCL design, arguing that technology, affordances, and infrastructure should be understood as emerging through relationships rather than as fixed properties. Drawing on two European research networks, the authors advocate for meso-level analysis bridging micro-group and macro-institutional processes, and recommend indirect design strategies that acknowledge contingency in how learners enact technological affordances within networked learning environments.

ijCSCL_2_2_0.title: A double issue for CSCL 2007
ijCSCL_2_2_0.authors: Gerry Stahl & Daniel D. Suthers & Friedrich Hesse
ijCSCL_2_2_0.summary_haiku: This editorial introduces a double issue of the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning coinciding with CSCL 2007. It presents papers organized around two "flash themes": scripting in collaborative learning environments and argumentation in CSCL. The collection features empirical studies employing mixed methods—quantitative coding, controlled experiments, and qualitative analysis—demonstrating how structured scripts and argumentative dialogue support knowledge construction in computer-mediated collaborative learning contexts.

ijCSCL_1_3_0.title: EDITORIAL Focusing on participation in group meaning making
ijCSCL_1_3_0.summary_haiku: This editorial proposes intersubjective meaning making as a unifying theoretical focus for CSCL research, arguing it better captures collaborative learning phenomena than traditional frameworks. The issue presents four articles exemplifying this approach: anchored discussion using quantitative analysis, networked handhelds supporting group interaction, and social network analysis combined with qualitative methods to examine student participation processes.

ijCSCL_8_1_1.title: Learning across levels
ijCSCL_8_1_1.summary_haiku: CSCL research must bridge individual, small-group, and community levels of analysis through emergent interactional resources. This theoretical framework proposes that resources—from ephemeral conversational moves to institutionalized practices—mediate across levels through processes of reification, sedimentation, and personalization. Empirical studies examining mathematical problem-solving, scientific representations, and collaborative learning demonstrate how tracking these resources reveals connections between local interactions and broader socio-cultural contexts.

ijCSCL_3_4_3.title: Exploring embedded guidance and self-efficacy in educational multi-user virtual environments
ijCSCL_3_4_3.authors: Brian C. Nelson & Diane Jass Ketelhut
ijCSCL_3_4_3.summary_haiku: This exploratory study examined how student self-efficacy in scientific inquiry affects guidance system use and learning outcomes in River City, an educational multi-user virtual environment. Using a sample of 96 middle school students, researchers found that students with low self-efficacy viewed significantly fewer guidance messages than higher-efficacy peers. While embedded reflective guidance improved learning across all efficacy levels, it only partially mitigated low self-efficacy's negative impact on performance. Notably, low-efficacy students with heavy guidance use achieved comparable outcomes to high-efficacy students without guidance.

ijCSCL_9_1_4.title: Explaining authors’ contribution to pivotal artifacts during mass collaboration in the Wikipedia’s knowledge base
ijCSCL_9_1_4.authors: Iassen Halatchliyski & Johannes Moskaliuk & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress
ijCSCL_9_1_4.summary_haiku: This empirical study examined how authors' contribution experience relates to their involvement in pivotal Wikipedia articles across two knowledge domains. Using network analysis on German Wikipedia data, researchers identified two types of pivotal articles: those central within single domains and those bridging domains. Results showed domain specialists predominantly contributed to domain-central articles, while generalists contributed to boundary-crossing articles. Article experience positively predicted contributions to both article types regardless of specialization.

ijCSCL_8_3_3.title: Advancing understanding using Nonaka’s model of knowledge creation and problem-based learning
ijCSCL_8_3_3.authors: Meng Yew Tee & Shuh Shing Lee
ijCSCL_8_3_3.summary_haiku: Integrating Nonaka's knowledge creation model with problem-based learning addresses Bereiter's critique that the model neglects understanding. This design-based research examined a 14-week course for in-service teachers developing technological pedagogical content knowledge. Findings demonstrate that combining socialization, externalization, combination, and internalization processes within problem-based learning phases cultivates advancing understanding of complex teaching-technology integration challenges.
